Dozens detained at authorized Communist Party rally after chants of 'Down with the Tsar'
Moscow police detained about 60 people at an authorized Communist Party rally on Oct. 4 after participants began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.
The rally marked the anniversary of Russia's 1993 constitutional crisis, when a standoff between President Boris Yeltsin and hard-line lawmakers culminated in the military shelling the parliament building in Moscow. Authorities said 123 people were killed, while unofficial estimates put the toll in the hundreds.
The Communist Party has organized annual events as a symbol of resistance to Yeltsin-era reforms, but this year's authorized rally took a turn as participants chanted slogans including "Freedom for political prisoners," "For fair elections," and "Down with the Tsar."
OVD-Info says participants also chanted “No to political repression,” “Down with Roskomnadzor,” and “Down with the party of crooks and thieves.”
The event had been authorized by Moscow authorities, but detentions reportedly intensified as the rally was ending and participants shifted toward more directly anti-Kremlin slogans.
According to OVD-Info, around 20 people were initially taken to Moscow's Krasnopresnenskiy police station before the reported total rose to about 60. The detainees were not all Communist Party supporters: 26 were Communist Party participants, 30 were members of the liberal Yabloko party, and several others were activists.
The Communist Party, Russia's main parliamentary opposition, generally aligns with the Kremlin on major national security and foreign policy issues, including support for Russia's war against Ukraine. It occasionally criticizes domestic policy but does not directly challenge President Vladimir Putin's rule.
Russia has pushed harder against political opposition and anti-war activism in recent years. In August, Russia's Supreme Court banned the Yabloko party from participating in upcoming parliamentary elections taking place Sept. 18-20. 
In September, authorities arrested members of the banned pro-peace Yabloko party, Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno and Grigory Grishin, among others, as part of a broader crackdown on dissent and political organizing.

OpenAI’s Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:25:00 UTC
08:25:00 KST

OpenAI’s Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes the benefits of AI justify accepting some risks and supports keeping the technology widely accessible to the public.
- Altman disagrees with stricter regulation proposals like those from rival Anthropic, calling such control "a completely unacceptable trade-off".
- The debate over AI risks continues, with Anthropic warning of potential dangers, while US officials oppose new restrictions to maintain competitiveness.
AI generated
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said in an interview with Politico’s technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: “I think there’s a lot of daylight.”
“I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ‘This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,’“ Altman said.
He called that “a completely unacceptable trade-off” that runs counter to the “lighter-touch regulatory stance” backed by OpenAI.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,’“ Altman said. “Because I think people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude more – good stuff than bad stuff.”
Altman’s remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to “pace the frontier,” a stance that Altman publicly endorsed.
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.
Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI’s potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers’ intentions and penetrate other companies’ systems.
The company said advanced models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours,” including attempts to “resist shutdown,” “conceal or manipulate information,” or generate outputs that could be interpreted as “coercive, deceptive, or manipulative”.
However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals.
He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed. REUTERS

Pacific leaders urge climate action as UN pre-COP talks open in Fiji
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

08:21:10 KST

Pacific leaders urge climate action as UN pre-COP talks open in Fiji
Pacific leaders urged action on climate change as UN pre-COP talks opened in Fiji's Nadi on Monday, ahead of next month's COP31 summit in Turkey. Discussions in Fiji and Tuvalu will focus on limiting warming to 1.5C, improving access to climate finance and protecting oceans as rising seas threaten communities.
The UN "pre-COP" climate gathering kicked off on Monday in the Fijian city of Nadi, where Pacific leaders are seeking to draw the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change.
The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming -- from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
This week's talks in Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit -- known as COP31 -- to be held next month in Turkey.
Pacific leaders are pushing for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C, enhance access to climate finance and give more attention to the impact on oceans.
"Our prime minister will carry three clear messages to the leaders this week: keep 1.5 degrees within reach, make finance reach the communities that need it and give the ocean its rightful place in the climate regime," Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya told the opening ceremony.
Sea levels are rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to a UN report.
Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, the report released in August said.
It also highlighted a financing gap, with developing countries needing $310-$365 billion to adapt, yet having only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
"Today in Fiji, we are again calling on the world to match ambition with delivery," said Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen, who is also president of negotiations for COP31.
He said talks at the pre-COP would focus on "capturing, capitalising on, and putting to work the knowledge of those who've been dealing with climate change here at its forefront, here at its cutting edge".
Regional leaders have pitched the pre-COP as a chance to bring the world to the Pacific.
Read moreColombia hosts climate talks in bid to lead global transition away from fossil fuels
Limited guest list
But officials have been forced to concede that the guest list will be smaller than they had hoped.
Fewer than a dozen world leaders have publicly confirmed that they will attend.
On the streets of Nadi, most locals seemed unaware that a global summit was even taking place.
Australia said last month 4,000 people from 60 nations would attend, without providing a full breakdown.
Among those attending will be Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal of Nepal, which is still reeling from August's Himalayan flood disaster which killed nearly 1,500 people and left 5,800 missing in Nepal and China.
Top delegates to the Pacific talks will also hold a one-day retreat on low-lying Tuvalu, already laying plans to relocate the population if it is consumed by the ocean.
The highest point in the capital Funafuti is just two metres (6.6 feet) above sea level, and two of its nine coral atolls are already largely swamped by rising waters.
Read moreWhat are the key takeaways from the COP30 climate summit?
'Act now decisively'
"Sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly ahead of the climate talks.
"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively, and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."
Only a handful of leaders are expected to join the Tuvalu leg of the trip.
"It does make you think nobody cares," said marine scientist Rajneel Singh, part of a team that reported large-scale coral death around Tuvalu.
"It's very, very sad."
As leader of the climate talks, major coal exporter Australia has faced accusations of hypocrisy.
Australian officials have insisted the country is rapidly expanding its renewable energy sources.
But activists accuse Australia of "double talk" on climate change, and have urged leaders to listen to Pacific communities most affected by global warming.
"As Australia prepares to chair the upcoming COP31 talks in partnership with the Pacific, it must do much more to turn empty rhetoric into real action to end the fossil fuel chokehold," Greenpeace's Shiva Gounden said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

All US B-1 bombers leave UK base after alleged Iran-linked plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:19:12 UTC
08:19:12 KST

The United States said Sunday that it had removed all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain following an alleged terror plot disrupted near the base last week that authorities suspect may have been linked to Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the aircraft, which were used among other missions for strikes on Iran during the war, were withdrawn because of security concerns surrounding the base.
About a dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at Fairford, northwest of London. Their removal could signal a change in how Washington intends to use the base, which Iran threatened to attack in July.
The aircraft have returned to bases in the United States, though the Pentagon stressed Sunday that they remain capable of providing a ‘global strike capability’ from US territory.
‘While operational security considerations prevented us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can now confirm that all US bombers deployed at Fairford have been redeployed to their home bases in the United States,’ the Pentagon said.
The unusual incident outside the base began early Sunday morning last week, when British police received a report of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward Fairford. Armed officers detained five British citizens in their 20s, all London residents, initially on suspicion of explosives-related offenses and later on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Dozens of nearby homes were evacuated and large police forces were deployed to the area.
The investigation later took an unexpected turn when police said no explosives had been found in the three vans, only gasoline. It was subsequently revealed that one of the suspects had called emergency services shortly before the arrests, adding further uncertainty over what had occurred.
All five suspects were released on bail under restrictive conditions, though police said they remain under investigation.
A sixth suspect, a young London resident with British-Iranian citizenship, was arrested Thursday on suspicion of planning terrorist acts. He was also released on bail several days later.
The suspects’ alleged plan remains unclear, but The Wall Street Journal reported that US officials had been aware of an Iran-linked plot to kill personnel at the base and damage the bombers stationed there.
A senior US official told the newspaper that a unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had recruited British citizens to carry out the attack, which allegedly involved several stages, including creating a diversion in a nearby area.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were ‘strong indications’ that Iran was involved in the incident, though the reported details of the alleged plot have not been officially confirmed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, said in an interview published Saturday by the Daily Mail that Israel had provided intelligence to Britain before the alleged attack was disrupted.

Britain set to levy tariffs on Chinese electric cars: Report
- Britain is considering tariffs on Chinese electric cars due to concerns over state-subsidised vehicles flooding the market, potentially matching the EU's 45% levy.
- British ministers aim to protect national interests and avoid negative impacts from the EU's 'Made in Europe' policy on the UK auto industry.
- UK officials seek to be recognised as a "trusted partner" by the EU to maintain trade flow and avoid barriers under new EU rules.
AI generated
LONDON - Britain is considering imposing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicle imports amid concerns that Beijing is flooding the market with state-subsidised cars, the Times newspaper reported on Oct 4.
Business minister Jonathan Reynolds is drawing up a package of potential tariffs on Chinese vehicle imports, the report said, citing concerns that Chinese manufacturers are “dumping” subsidised vehicles into Britain.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Asked to comment, a spokesperson from the British government told Reuters no tariffs have been imposed on Chinese EVs.
“We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests,” the spokesperson said in an e-mail.
British ministers are ready to match the European Union’s 45% levy on Chinese electric cars, the Times said, to avoid the pain of “Made in Europe” proposals, which could impact UK companies selling into the EU.
The EU’s “Made in Europe” policy is aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese components by prioritising European-made goods, raising concerns among British auto makers that supply parts into European manufacturing chains and sell vehicles across the bloc.
Burnham said in September he would make the case that Britain should be treated as a “trusted partner” under the proposed EU rules, warning that excluding the UK could damage its car industry.
The Financial Times reported in September that Brussels had urged British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to align more closely with EU trade policy and raise tariffs on Chinese cars if Britain wants to avoid the “made in Europe” barriers.
According to the Times, citing senior government sources, ministers believe any decision on tariffs should be based on Britain’s national interest rather than automatically following the EU’s lead. REUTERS

Iran’s oil minister resigns, president appoints replacement
Unknown

23:02:59 UTC
08:02:59 KST

Tolga Akbaba, Sami Sohta and Rania Abushamala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, Iran’s state-run Tasnim news agency reported Sunday, citing a presidential official.
Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy head of communications at the Iranian president’s office, said President Masoud Pezeshkian has accepted Paknejad’s resignation.
Hamid Bovard has been appointed acting oil minister to oversee the ministry’s affairs, Tabatabaei added.
No reason was given for Paknejad’s resignation, which came amid unprecedented US sanctions on Iran, particularly targeting its oil sector.
Bovard previously served as the head of the state-run National Iranian Oil Company and has spent most of his career working in oilfield operations.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Saturday that Iran has no oil shipments remaining at sea and will generate zero oil revenue this week.
On Aug. 25, the US Treasury Department announced the launch of Operation Economic Outcast, a broad campaign aimed at completely isolating Iran from the global financial system.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic route for energy supplies. The US military later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Efforts to end the war have continued since a June framework deal which seeks to pave the way for a final peace agreement covering navigation through the strategic waterway and Iran’s nuclear program.

Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

A looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies, the Unite union has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache.
The union said Apache workers had “emphatically” backed strike action after being given what it said was an unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was “raking in eye-watering profits”.
Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, “leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket”.
Apache said it had “engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions” and added that it had offered a 4% pay increase for staff, “whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year”.
Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators.
Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, “being brought to a standstill”, Unite said.
That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – “going down”, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators.
Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have “far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers”.
Consumers have already been grappling with rising fuel and gas prices because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf.
On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel had climbed to a record £2 a litre.
At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.
Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.”
Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms “would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies”.
The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year.
“We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,” Apache said. “The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.”
Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping “experienced personnel” on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages.
“As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,” Apache added.
Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite, were called off this summer after they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July.
Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.

Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows.
In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.
The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.
However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.
The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.
Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam.
Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.
Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.”
She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”.
Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

Flavio Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election heads to runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Flavio Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election heads to runoff
Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff, with right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, leading incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
With 88% of polling stations reporting, Bolsonaro had received 48.19% of the vote, compared with Lula’s 43.81%, according to the official tally.
Under Brazilian election rules, a presidential candidate must secure more than 50% of valid votes to win in the first round. With neither Bolsonaro nor Lula reaching that threshold, the two will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
The election is widely seen as a highly polarized contest over Brazil’s political direction, pitting Lula’s left-wing agenda against Bolsonaro’s conservative platform, which emphasizes tougher measures against crime and the protection of “traditional values.”
The vote also presents a foreign-policy choice, as Lula has sought to strengthen Brazil’s role in BRICS and deepen ties with China and other Global South powers, while Bolsonaro has emphasized closer relations with Washington and touted his ties to US President Donald Trump.
Lula served as Brazil’s president from 2003 to 2011 and returned to office for a third term in 2023. He was barred from running in the 2018 election due to a corruption conviction and spent 580 days in prison. Brazil’s Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021, ruling that the court that tried him lacked jurisdiction, restoring his political rights and allowing him to run again.
Jair Bolsonaro, who served as president from 2019 to 2022, is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of attempting a coup following his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election. Both men have denied wrongdoing in their respective cases and argued that the prosecutions against them were politically motivated.
Bolsonaro’s other son, Eduardo, has lived in self-imposed exile in the United States since 2025. Brazil’s Supreme Court sentenced him in June to four years and two months in prison for coercion after finding that he had sought US pressure on Brazilian authorities in an effort to interfere with his father’s coup trial.
Brazilian authorities have also investigated alleged US interference in the country’s politics after Trump denounced the case against Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch hunt,” while Flavio and Eduardo Bolsonaro met the US president at the White House in May.
The election also brought victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family, with former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro elected to the Senate from the Federal District and Bolsonaro’s third son, Carlos, winning a Senate seat in Santa Catarina.

Search continues for missing Bermuda to Boston flight as crews plan to comb seabed
The air ambulance carrying 6 people disappeared on Saturday. Searchers said they had found a ‘debris field’ off the Massachusetts coast
A search continued on Sunday off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston as authorities planned to comb the seabed, the US Coast Guard said.
The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the coastguard at 2am on Saturday saying it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later on Saturday found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Coast Guard Northeast District Rear Admiral Matt Lake said at a news conference on Sunday.
Coastguard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities have since searched an area encompassing 7,356 sq km (2,840 square miles) using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters.
“This is a large and demanding search area,” Lake said.

US withdraws all B-1 bombers from British military base RAF Fairford
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that all US B-1 bombers deployed to Britain’s RAF Fairford had returned home following a security incident that prompted nearby evacuations. Police found no explosives after reports of suspicious activity at the base last Sunday. Five London-based British men arrested were subsequently released on bail.
The Pentagon confirmed reports Sunday that the United States has withdrawn all B-1 bomber planes from Royal Air Force Fairford, the UK airbase where a suspicious incident triggered nearby evacuations.
A statement from a Pentagon official said "we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
Police were called to the base in southwest England last Sunday after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
Read moreMystery over UK airbase scare as police find petrol but no explosives
The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used to launch strikes on Iran.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
Investigators said they did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," National Counter Terrorism Policing head Lawrence Taylor said.
The five London-based Britons arrested in the incident, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
"I wouldn't have done that," US President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved.
Read moreUK police arrest dual UK-Iranian national over Fairford air base incident
Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base.
Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 5. /TASS/. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is leading with 49.58% of the vote in the first round of Brazil's presidential election and does not have the absolute majority anymore, according to data from the Superior Electoral Court.
64.81% of the electronic ballots have been processed thus far.
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva continues to close the gap and come in second with 42.25% of the votes cast. Over 79.3 mln votes have been counted for the time being.
The drop of Bolsonaro’s result below 50% confirms that the winner will not be determined in the first round of the election and the candidates will go for the second round, Folha de S. Paulo newspaper said.

One person was killed and six injured, as Russian forces carried out a double-tap strike using Banderol missiles in Kharkiv’s industrial district.

Banderol missiles have been a part of Russia's increasing use of jet-powered loitering munitions, combining features of a cruise missile and a jet-powered drone. Its speed, maneuverability, and low-altitude flight profile can make the Banderol difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
After a July 8 Banderol missile struck Kharkiv, Spartak Borysenko, head of the department for combating crimes committed in the context of armed conflict at the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office, told Suspilne Kharkiv that the munition can reach speeds of up to 800 kilometers (500 miles) per hour and carry around 300–400 kilograms (660–880 pounds) of explosives.
"It has a guidance system and numerous control surfaces, and it can change its direction and altitude while in flight," Borysenko said.
On Sept. 24, three Russian S-8000 Banderol missiles struck a farm in Kharkiv Oblast, killing 6 and injuring 14.
Kharkiv has also faced repeated attacks with other Russian aerial weapons in recent days. On Oct. 2, Russian glide bombs struck the city’s Slobidskyi and Nemyshlianskyi districts, killing two women and injuring 36 people, including three children.
The latest strike is evidence of Russia’s increasing use of fast, maneuverable jet-powered munitions against targets in Ukraine, adding further strain to air defenses already contending with drones, glide bombs, and missiles.

Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:36:54 UTC
07:36:54 KST

Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
The country’s crackdown on human rights has left it increasingly isolated in Latin America.
Nicaragua’s government has announced it will withdraw from the Central American Parliament, a key regional body, as President Daniel Ortega and his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo, consolidate power.
The Foreign Ministry announced on Saturday that it would exit the six-country parliament, established to help promote human rights and democracy in Central America.
The announcement comes shortly after Friday’s passage of a resolution at the Organization of American States (OAS), calling on Nicaragua to restore civil rights and release political prisoners.
The Nicaraguan government, however, said Saturday’s action was “in the full exercise of its sovereignty”.
The government said the decision would take effect immediately, the latest in a series of withdrawals from regional and international organisations the country has undertaken.
The Ortega-Murillo government has accused such international groups of being vehicles for outside intervention.
Nicaragua pulled out of the OAS in 2023 and the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHCR) in 2025 over criticisms of the country’s human rights record, which has deteriorated during Ortega’s tenure.
Ortega has been accused of using the state to target critics and dissidents, including through imprisonment, torture and exile.
A UN report released in September found the government was responsible for at least eight deaths in custody since 2018, when Ortega began a sharp crackdown on protests and dissent.
The report also detailed inconsistencies in the government’s account of in-custody deaths, including that of Indigenous Miskito leader Brooklyn Rivera.
A critic of the Ortega government, Rivera was detained for 32 months with minimal contact with his family before dying in May.
The government blamed his death on the effects of a previous case of COVID-19, an assessment the Physicians for Human Rights group called “not medically coherent”.
“A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance,” said Jan-Michael Simon, the group’s chair.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has also been vocal in denouncing the Nicaraguan government’s abuses, including Rivera’s death.
In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio published a statement calling Nicaragua’s government a “dictatorship” after it announced it would abolish the country’s upcoming elections.
He also framed the Ortega-Murillo government as a threat to US national security. “Ortega’s pledge to abolish elections in Nicaragua proves his cowardice and fear of the Nicaraguan people’s will,” Rubio wrote.
But the Trump administration has come under criticism for seeking to deport Nicaraguan citizens who were expelled under Ortega’s leadership.
Human Rights Watch recently warned that the Trump administration had detained eight Nicaraguan nationals for deportation, seven of whom were among 222 political prisoners flown into exile in the US in February 2023, during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Nicaragua subsequently stripped them of their citizenship and branded them as “traitors” to the country. The Ortega government also seized any property they had in the country.
Human Rights Watch urged the Trump administration not to deport the eight detainees, warning that they could face abuse if they were returned to Nicaragua. Four of the detainees reportedly have pending asylum cases.
“After offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government just three years ago, the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them,” Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.
“International law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of persecution or torture. US authorities should not be trying to send these men back into danger.”

US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears

Unknown Publisher

22:23:30 UTC

US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several ‘terrorism-related’ arrests were made outside RAF Fairford.
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain — it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia in March.

FBI arrests woman accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:21:52 UTC

FBI arrests alleged Chinese agent at LAX after she allegedly surveilled son of Taiwanese president
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.
Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.
Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.
The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.
Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.
Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.
Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.
The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.
New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.
In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

Nationalist Parties, Dodik Dominate Bosnian Election Amid Low Turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:20:58 UTC
07:20:58 KST

SARAJEVO -- Milorad Dodik, the Russia-friendly former leader of Bosnia-Herzegovina's Serbian-led entity, declared victory for his party in the region, with nationalist parties also scoring wins in Bosnia's complex electoral system -- results likely to keep tensions high in the country and the region.
"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka late on October 4, saying preliminary figures assure that his SNSD -- the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats -- will remain in power in Republika Srpska (RS).
Voters cast ballots for the country's central tripartite presidency and national parliament, alongside regional legislative races, such as in the RS, in a complex political system set up under the Dayton accords that ended the country's devastating 1992-95 war.
As part of the Dayton agreements, Bosnia was divided into two semi-autonomous entities -- the Serb-run RS and a Muslim Bosniak-Croat federation -- linked by a sometimes weak central government.
In his victory speech, Dodik said the SNSD’s Zeljka Cvijanovic will become a member of Bosnia's tripartite presidency, based on results with 92 percent of ballots counted.
Pro-West incumbent Denis Becirovic was on course to win the Bosniak seat in the presidency and is expected to be joined by Darijana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), who is projected to win the Croat seat.
At 39, Filipovic is set to become the youngest member of the Bosnian presidency since the end of the 1992-95 conflict.
Thanks For Trump, Putin
Dodik, who has pushed for greater autonomy from the state government for the Serbian entity -- often along with secessionist rhetoric -- was quick to thank the US and Russian presidents for the victory.
"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory...we would probably be political corpses today," he told supporters.
"But now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners," he said, also offering thanks to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Our political positions remain firm and we will not abandon them. We will continue working for the benefit of our people," Dodik said.
Dodik, 67, was not on any ballot, having been banned from public office, but his face was visible on billboards across Republika Srpska, where he remains a highly influential voice.
Dodik and other RS officials previously faced US sanctions over allegations related to violations of the Dayton peace accords that ended Bosnia's 1992-95 war and for refusing to implement actions of an international peace envoy.
However, the US Treasury Department announced on October 29, 2025, that Dodik and dozens of his allies had been removed from the US sanctions list.
The Treasury did not elaborate on the move, but it followed Washington’s statement welcoming the appointment of an interim president to replace Dodik, who had been stripped of his presidency after a court ruling.
Throughout his tenure as RS president, Dodik faced criticism for authoritarian tendencies, undermining democratic institutions, and fostering a culture of political patronage.
In one preelection rally, Dodik called for the border between RS and Serbia to be erased. Other nationalist politicians have called for a merger with Serbia.
SDA Leads Parliament Vote
Meanwhile, ethnic-nationalist forces appear to have scored success in the BiH’s national parliament in Sarajevo on October 4.
According to preliminary results, the nationalist Party of Democratic Action (SDA) has the largest number of votes in the federation parliament, trailed by the Social Democratic Party of BiH (SDP-BH), and the Croatian Democratic Union of BiH (HDZ BiH).
The SNSD and Dodik are openly pro-Russian and anti-NATO, while the SDA, HDZ, and SDP are pro-EU and favor NATO.
Outgoing Croat presidency member Zeljko Komsic said the strong results by nationalist parties reflected growing ethnic consolidation among voters.
"It is evident that ethnic homogenization of the electorate has taken place across all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina," Komsic said, adding that the election suggested that "the idea of a civic state currently lacks broad electoral support."
While the political divide still reflects the 1990s conflict, a new element in this election was biometric voter checks and ballot scanners. This led to some polling stations opening later than scheduled amid technical hiccups.
Bosnia is the first country in the Western Balkans to implement the system nationwide, a measure imposed by the international High Representative's Office as part of election-integrity reforms under the framework established by the Dayton accords.

American bomber fleet departs Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:17:02 BST
07:17:02 KST

All US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have returned to their home stations in the United States, ending the latest sustained deployment of American heavy bombers at the British airbase, according to US European Command.
European Command confirmed on 4 October that the aircraft “are redeploying to their home stations”, while a US Department of Defense official separately confirmed that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had now left the base.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” a US Air Force statement said.
The aircraft remaining at Fairford before the departure were B-1B Lancer bombers. The New York Times, citing two US officials, reported that 12 B-1s were involved in the redeployment and that at least three had reached South Dakota by Sunday. No reason for the withdrawal has been given publicly by the Pentagon or US European Command.
European Command said American bombers routinely deploy internationally as part of global readiness and operational requirements, without providing further detail on the decision to bring the Fairford aircraft home. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements,” the US statement said.
The service added that its bomber force remained capable of carrying out long-range operations directly from the continental United States. “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime.”
RAF Fairford is a Royal Air Force station used extensively by the United States Air Force and serves as a forward operating location for US strategic bomber deployments to Europe. Its long runway and supporting infrastructure allow aircraft including the B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress to operate from the Gloucestershire base.
The airfield has hosted a substantial US bomber presence during 2026. B-1 and B-52 aircraft operated from Fairford during American military operations connected with the war with Iran, making the base one of the principal European locations supporting the deployment of US long-range strike aircraft.
Six B-52 Stratofortress bombers had already departed Fairford earlier in the year, leaving B-1 Lancers as the remaining deployed bomber force at the base by the beginning of October.
The B-1B is a supersonic long-range conventional bomber operated by the US Air Force. Although originally developed during the Cold War with a nuclear role, the aircraft was subsequently converted to a conventional-only mission and has been used extensively for long-range strike operations.

UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:08:16 BST
07:08:16 KST

Royal Navy patrol ships HMS Spey and HMS Tamar are to enter the South China Sea for a ten-day multinational exercise with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, continuing a British naval presence in waters where Beijing has repeatedly objected to UK military activity and policy, according to the Royal Navy.
The two Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels will take part in Exercise Bersama Lima 26, the annual tri-service exercise conducted under the Five Power Defence Arrangements, or FPDA, which links the United Kingdom with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore.
Bersama Lima, meaning “Together Five” in Malay, will involve ships, aircraft and troops operating across maritime, land and air scenarios. Forces committed to the exercise include frigates, patrol vessels, a corvette, tanker and submarine, as well as divers and specialist boarding teams.
Australian F-35A Lightning II fighters will lead the air element of the exercise, while planned scenarios include troops directing naval gunfire, boarding and searching vessels at sea, anti-submarine warfare and naval air defence supported by participating air forces.
The deployment takes place against a long-running dispute between Beijing and several regional governments over territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea, as well as wider disagreements over the activities of military forces from countries outside the region. China has repeatedly criticised British involvement. In 2018, Beijing said it had lodged stern representations with the UK after HMS Albion sailed close to the Paracel Islands, which China calls the Xisha Islands. China said the ship had entered waters it regarded as its territorial sea without permission, while Britain has consistently maintained the importance of navigational rights under international law.
Beijing again objected in 2021 as the UK increased its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific, accusing Britain of deploying its Carrier Strike Group to the South China Sea to “flex its naval muscles”. More recently, in July 2026, the Chinese Embassy in London strongly condemned the UK for joining an international statement supporting the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award and urged Britain to stop what it described as “stirring up trouble” in the region.
HMS Tamar has also recently conducted a freedom-of-navigation activity in the South China Sea. In a parliamentary answer published on 8 September, the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the patrol ship operated alongside the Royal Australian Navy on 1 September as part of the UK’s stated commitment to freedom of navigation and overflight under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The Royal Navy says HMS Spey and HMS Tamar have themselves conducted freedom-of-navigation missions in disputed waters during their five-year deployment to the Indo-Pacific, sometimes operating independently and sometimes alongside regional partners.
Before Bersama Lima moves into its main operational phase, personnel from the five participating nations will spend time familiarising themselves with different vessels, equipment, procedures and terminology, while senior officers carry out planning for the live exercise.
According to a Royal Navy news update, Lieutenant Commander Cheryl Goodwin, HMS Tamar’s Executive Officer, said: “We’re looking forward to being a part of Bersama Lima 26 – an exercise which unites some of our closest allies, tests the crew in a traditional war-fighting role, and demonstrates the UK’s resolve to maintain stability in the Indo-Pacific region through supporting our partners.”
HMS Tamar is also carrying a Royal New Zealand Navy boarding team during the exercise, adding another element of direct integration between the participating forces.
Lieutenant Williams, a Royal New Zealand Navy officer embarked aboard Tamar, said: “It’s a first for me and my team, but it’s a well-trodden path which has been established through a deep history of our navies working together.”
He added: “We’ve got a lot of experience to share, are always looking to improve and we’re ready to go.”
The Five Power Defence Arrangements were established in 1971 and provide a framework for defence cooperation between the five member states. Regular exercises bring together naval, land and air forces, particularly around Malaysia and Singapore, to practise combined operations and develop common procedures. Both British patrol ships have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021. Their mission, known as Operation Highwall, has included multinational exercises, maritime security operations, sanctions enforcement, humanitarian assistance, defence engagement and freedom-of-navigation activity.
Bersama Lima marks a return to operations for HMS Spey after the vessel spent the summer undergoing maintenance in Singapore. HMS Tamar has remained active across the region, including participation in the US-led Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise and a visit to Cambodia before its September activity with the Royal Australian Navy in the South China Sea.
The ships passed five years continuously deployed to the Indo-Pacific in September, making them the first Royal Navy vessels to maintain a persistent presence in the region since the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.
During Bersama Lima, Spey and Tamar will operate as part of a larger multinational force, with the live phase testing the five FPDA nations across areas including maritime interdiction, anti-submarine warfare and air defence in and around the South China Sea.

He expressed hope SC would rise to the occasion and rectify the mistakes prevailing in the system.He said around 93% of adjudicated cases of deleted voters in West Bengal had been decided in their favour which meant they were illegally removed. TOI had first reported on September 20 that appellate tribunals had upheld deletion of only 8,649 voters out of the 1.2 lakh cases decided so far."Now, the unfortunate part is that all this came before the court very recently. Two judges differed, and the ultimate thing is now it has gone before a bench, probably of five judges, in order to find out whether this is good law or not... But meanwhile, these appointments continue only in the hands of govt of the day. Now, we saw the danger of this happening very recently. All of you have seen that in the Bengal elections, 90 lakh voters were disenfranchised.
That is an astounding figure. Ninety lakh voters getting disenfranchised did not somehow move Supreme Court enough to stay this," Justice Nariman said.Out of those who were disenfranchised, around 22 lakh filed appeals, the former SC judge said, adding, "The others must be people who don't have the wherewithal or access to justice."
Justice Nariman pointed out that of 1 lakh appeals, almost all were decided in favour of the voters. "So, you can imagine this was completely illegal - knocking out of the common man, the citizen of India in order that a govt obtains what it wants. And in Bengal, we saw it ousted govt of the day and brought in govt of Centre. Now, these are very, very disturbing things that are happening in our country today," he said, speaking on 'The Constitution and the Common Man' at Rajkumar College, Rajkot."I hope the apex court, the institution to which I once belonged, steps in immediately and rectifies these things. You can't have an EC which functions or malfunctions like this. So the first important red flag qua the Constitution and the common man is the appointment process of election commissioners. The sooner the constitution bench decides you have to have somebody like a PM, leader of the opposition coupled with the Chief Justice or his nominee, who then picks the best names in order to see that votes actually translate into what they were supposed to translate into happens," Justice Nariman said.

Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia issue declaration on Red Sea governance, state sovereignty, water rights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:04:15 CST
07:04:15 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The leaders of Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia on Sunday issued a joint declaration on state sovereignty, Red Sea governance, and water rights, stressing the necessity of adhering to international law as the foundation for regional stability and cooperation.
In the El Alamein Joint Declaration issued following the quadrilateral consultative summit in Egypt's New Alamein, the leaders rejected interference in the internal affairs of the region's states "under any pretext."
The summit was attended by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, and Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan, chairman of Sudan's Transitional Sovereign Council.
The leaders discussed regional and international developments, and ways to strengthen political, economic, trade and cultural cooperation among the four countries, and addressed a number of regional issues.
On Sudan, the leaders support the unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national institutions of the Republic of Sudan, rejecting the establishment of any parallel entities.
They reject any recognition of or support for the so-called "Somaliland" and affirm that the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states.
The declaration also stressed the importance of respecting international law regarding transboundary rivers, including the Nile River, particularly the principle of "no harm" and the obligation to cooperate through prior notification, consultation, and consensus.
They categorically reject "any unilateral measures that harm the existing water uses of the two downstream Nile states."
The summit came amid growing Egyptian efforts to strengthen coordination with countries in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region over regional security and stability. ■

News Analysis: British PM reopens Brexit debate, but return to EU remains uncertain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:04:08 CST
07:04:08 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Feng, Chen Shulin
LONDON, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reopened the debate over Britain's relationship with the European Union (EU), putting eventual membership among the options.
His remarks challenge Labour's previous red lines and raise a central question: how far is Britain prepared to go in rebuilding ties with the bloc?
In his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister on Tuesday, Burnham said "Brexit has done more harm than good," and laid out options for "Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners."
In an interview broadcast by the BBC the next day, he said rejoining the EU was one option. "I would like to see Britain rejoin in my lifetime," he said, but added that he would "look at the different options."
Those options range from maintaining the current relationship to joining a customs union, participating in the single market or returning to full EU membership. They involve different degrees of economic integration and political commitment.
The openness to reconsidering those options contrasts with Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out returning to the single market or customs union and restoring freedom of movement. Burnham had also previously pledged not to reopen "divisive arguments about rejoining the EU," according to the Financial Times.
The debate comes a decade after 52 percent of voters backed leaving the EU in the June 2016 referendum. Britain formally left in 2020.
ECONOMIC CASE, POLITICAL RISKS
Burnham has made economic growth a critical argument for reconsidering Britain's relationship with the EU.
"I think we have seen growth harmed by Brexit and it's hard to see how we can get back to the higher levels of growth we once had by staying too distant from our largest market," he said in an interview broadcast by ITV News on Wednesday.
Polling also points to public support for closer ties, although that does not necessarily amount to a mandate for full membership.
A Public First poll found that 70 percent of British voters wanted the government to build a closer relationship with the EU, the Independent reported Wednesday. YouGov data published on the same day showed 59 percent support for rejoining the EU.
Reopening the debate also carries political risks. Labour MP Graham Stringer said it would be a "betrayal" for Britain to go back on the vote, and warned that the debate could be "more acrimonious" than in 2016.
WELCOME SIGNALS, BUT NO EASY RETURN
French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the prospect of Britain's return. Macron said in English, "welcome back," describing a possible British return to the EU as great news for Britain and Europe.
Sanchez said Brexit had been a "huge loss" for both the British people and the EU.
Those responses signal political goodwill, but they do not establish agreement across the bloc on the conditions for British membership.
Rejoining would require negotiations over membership terms, the European Parliament's consent, unanimous approval by the Council of the EU and ratification of an accession treaty by Britain and all EU member states. Support from individual European leaders would be only part of that process.
A forthcoming UK-EU summit could provide an early indication of how Burnham intends to translate his remarks into policy. The summit originally scheduled for July was postponed and could be held in November. British media have suggested that Burnham wants it also to address the broader framework of UK-EU relations.
The immediate test is whether the government sets out a concrete negotiating position. That would help clarify whether Burnham is pursuing closer practical cooperation or preparing for a more fundamental change in Britain's relationship with the EU. ■

IDF kills suspected infiltrator approaching post in southern Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:48:21 UTC
06:48:21 KST

Israeli troops shot and killed a man suspected of trying to infiltrate an IDF post in southern Syria overnight, the military said Monday.
The incident occurred in an Israeli-controlled security zone near the Syrian village of al-Hamidiyah, close to the border with Israel. The man approached one of the military posts in the area, prompting Carmeli Brigade troops to begin a standard procedure for confronting a suspected intruder.
According to the military, the man continued climbing an embankment toward the post despite orders to stop and was eventually shot and killed outside the position.
The IDF said it was investigating the incident, including whether the man was armed and attempting to carry out an attack. No Israeli troops were injured.
“A short while ago, IDF soldiers identified a suspect attempting to infiltrate an IDF post in the Security Zone in southern Syria,” the military said shortly after the incident. “Following a quick identification, the soldiers fired toward the suspect and eliminated him. No IDF injuries were reported.”
“The IDF will continue to operate in the Security Zone in southern Syria in order to remove any threat to Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers,” it added.
The incident began when soldiers at one of the observation posts spotted a person climbing an embankment outside the military position. The troops called on him to stop and said he appeared to be holding something in his hand.
The man did not comply and continued advancing, according to the soldiers, prompting them to open fire. He was killed in the shooting.
Troops were searching the surrounding area afterward to rule out the presence of additional suspects.
A reserve officer serving in the buffer zone in Syria told ynet that it was not the first incident in recent weeks involving people approaching IDF positions.
“They are testing the area,” the officer said. “They send people, they send cells, they do all kinds of things to see where we operate and how we respond.”
“It reminds me of the period before Oct. 7,” he added, referring to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. “Disturbances, one person here, another person there. They see how long it takes you to respond, how you respond and from where you detect them.”
Several weeks ago, another Syrian man, allegedly armed with a knife, was suspected of attempting to infiltrate one of the IDF posts in the buffer zone and was detained. An investigation later determined that he was suffering from mental illness.

Iran says no military solution to war as peace talks with US stall

A UK maritime agency reported another tanker hit by an unidentified projectile.
Iran's top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States' war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran's attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
Read moreG7 members will release 100 million barrels of diesel after US threatens export ban
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz "reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room", though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
In Iran, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, the president's office said on Sunday, as the US maintains a blockade on the country's oil exports.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had asked Paknejad to continue in his post but was now accepting his departure as the minister had insisted on leaving, the official added.
Paknejad has been replaced by Hamid Bovard, the chief executive of the National Iranian Oil Company, the presidency said.
Focused on Hormuz
Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.

"The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures," he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA.
"Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario."

The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.
