Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:39:55 UTC
06:39:55 KST

Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including the ‘voluntary intoxication’ rule at the heart of the Cornell case.
Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024.
Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses.
But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York.
While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice.
Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work.
“These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said.
She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations.
“It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said.
Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case.
On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session.
Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis.
“I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.”
Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform.
Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend:
‘Voluntary intoxication’ statute
The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “voluntary intoxication” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap.
“It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent.
That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”.
That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine.
The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure.
New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases.
But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs.
“I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera.
Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators.
“We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera.
In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily.
But the legislation has yet to be taken up in the state Assembly.
The rape-shield gap
New York’s rape-shield protections limit the use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history and conduct in criminal proceedings. But those protections do not currently extend to civil cases.
This distinction could matter in the Cornell case because Doe filed a civil lawsuit.
Vladimer said questions about a survivor’s behaviour could come up in the discovery process of a civil case, as well as in court.
“There is the potential of her having to face questions about things like her sexual history,” Vladimer said.
Bridie Farrell, the director of victim rights advocacy and legislation at the law firm Weitz and Luxenberg, told Al Jazeera that she has seen major differences in how male and female survivors are questioned in civil cases where this practice is still permitted.
In one case involving a brother and sister who were both sexually assaulted, Farrell said the man was not questioned about his sexual history while the woman was “grilled on it”.
A bill sponsored by State Senator Liz Krueger would extend rape-shield protections to civil proceedings. The measure passed the Senate in June and is currently before the Assembly Judiciary Committee.
Retaliatory defamation lawsuits
Advocates are also pushing for legislation to prevent retaliatory defamation lawsuits.
Boylan said she has spent more than $2m defending herself in legal proceedings connected to her accusations against Cuomo, who stepped down as New York governor in 2021.
He has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing, despite a state attorney general’s report that concluded he “engaged in conduct constituting sexual harassment”.
“Every step of the way, we have a system that penalises people for speaking up about their own harm,” Boylan said.
Boylan and Charlotte Bennett, a former aide who also accused Cuomo of sexual harassment, are proponents of the Speak Your Truth Act, which would provide legal protections for people who publicly report sexual assault, harassment or discrimination.
The bill, sponsored by Assembly member Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, would make certain communications about sexual assault, harassment or discrimination privileged when they are made without malice.
It would also allow survivors of sexual misconduct who successfully defend themselves against a defamation lawsuit to recover legal fees and costs. The bill remains in an Assembly committee.
A recent win, a long way to go
For Bridie Farrell, the victims’ rights advocate, the fight for legal change is personal.
Farrell was a 15-year-old competitive speed skater in 1997 when she said she was sexually abused by her 33-year-old teammate and mentor. She came forward with her story of abuse in 2013.
By then, the statute of limitations in her case had expired. Farrell later became an advocate for changes to New York’s laws, helping to pass the Child Victims Act in 2019 that extended the time available for survivors of childhood sexual abuse to pursue criminal and civil claims.
The law allowed Farrell to file her own case, which she did in 2020. She tells Al Jazeera that a trial has finally been scheduled for June 2027.
“Before we passed the Child Victims Act in 2019, New York was one of the worst in the country,” Farrell said of the situation for sexual assault survivors seeking justice.
Farrell considers the legal impediments to Doe’s case — like the “voluntary intoxication” statute — all too predictable. “I’m not surprised if we haven’t updated a law that is archaic,” she said.
Still, lawmakers have signalled willingness to reform such laws. In announcing the state Assembly’s working group on sexual-assault laws, Speaker Carl Heastie pledged to “thoughtfully” consider how the state can strengthen its laws.
“The allegations being reported out of Cornell University are truly horrifying,” Heastie said on Wednesday. “We want to do everything we can to ensure victims of sexual assault see justice served.”
But survivors and sexual violence advocates say the Cornell case points to problems that go beyond any single law. They hope to see widespread systemic and societal change.
“Changing legislation is incredibly important. But legislation in a lot of cases can only go [as far as] the paper that it’s written on,” Boylan said. “It would be amiss to orient this horrible, tragic, unacceptable, infuriating case in isolation without looking at the broader rape culture of our state and our country.”

Brazilian presidential election polls close amid economic worries, corruption scandals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:36:45 UTC
06:36:45 KST

Senator Flavio Bolsonaro held a narrowing lead in the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, after more than half the votes were counted, with pollster Datafolha projecting that the election would proceed to a second vote.
Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power, was leading leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
With nearly 85% of votes reported, Flavio led Lula with 48.47% of the votes to the president's 43.49%. A candidate must pass 50% in order to win outright in the first round.
Private surveys in the run up to the election had forecast Lula leading the first-round vote by around 3 percentage points.
The two leading candidates were expected to head into a second-round vote, Brazilian pollster Datafolha said. Surveys have shown Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in an October 25 runoff.
Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula's northeast stronghold have been tallied more slowly.
Analysts told Reuters they believed Flavio was receiving "protest votes" of people voting against Lula rather than for the right-wing senator - votes they had been expected to save until a second round.
A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
All of Brazil's states close polls at 5:00 p.m. Brasilia time, though voters in line before this time will still be allowed to cast their vote. Results will be reported shortly after.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in a likely runoff.
While polls right up until Saturday showed Lula would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters' frustration with his chief opponent.
Flavio was counting on "a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula," he said. "I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the first round."
Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula's Workers Party out of office.
"I don't think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes," she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate.
Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Flavio despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state.
Officials warn of US refusing to recognize election results
On the other hand, Lula's allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to send US officials to Brazil.
"What is at stake is the future of Brazil," Lula said after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
"I'm a little worried about everything that's been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections," said Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for Lula and preferred to withhold his surname.
"We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty," said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore outfits supporting the president.
As of Sunday afternoon, the election was proceeding normally, Brazil's electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference.
“Teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever," he said.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs.
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising public debt, fiscal concerns, key issue in Brazil election
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.
"I voted for Brazil to start growing again," said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Lula voter who moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Sunday.
"The best social program is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth," he said.
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker's ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker's connections to Moraes, widely perceived as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case against him is politically motivated for his role in the conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
On Sunday, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former president Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

Nearly three years after Oct. 7, Israeli donations keep climbing as philanthropy shifts to recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:36:05 UTC
06:36:05 KST

Nearly three years after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 massacre, Israel’s philanthropic sector is showing signs that the surge in charitable giving triggered by the attack has become more than a temporary emergency response. According to Ori Ben-Shlomo, CEO of Israeli donation platform JGive, donations have continued to rise even as the country has moved from immediate wartime relief toward long-term rehabilitation.
In the days after October 7, normal life across Israel was upended. Soldiers were called into reserve duty, hundreds of thousands of Israelis were evacuated, families sought assistance, nonprofits scrambled to identify urgent needs, and private citizens stepped in as state systems struggled to respond.
At the same time, an unprecedented wave of donations began flowing into Israel. Israelis and Jews abroad sought ways to quickly support evacuees, soldiers, affected families, and organizations providing food, equipment, housing, and other emergency assistance, turning digital fundraising platforms into a central part of the civilian response.
Nearly three years later, the questions facing the sector have changed. Diaspora Jewish communities are balancing support for Israel with mounting needs at home, emergency fundraising has increasingly given way to rehabilitation, and Israelis themselves appear to have developed a different relationship with philanthropy.
Ben-Shlomo said JGive’s figures indicate that the shift has endured.
“I think it tells the story of Israeli society through our eyes,” Ben-Shlomo said. “In the year before October 7, 2023, around NIS 160 million passed through our platform. When October 7 came, that rose to something like NIS 330 million in donations. We are talking about hundreds of thousands of donors a year.”
The initial increase was dramatic, but JGive executives did not know whether it would last. During the first months of the war, most donations went toward immediate needs, including food, supplies, assistance for evacuees, and support for soldiers.
“At a certain point, when the immediate emergency began to subside, we thought perhaps the burst of generosity, from Israel and abroad, would also fade,” Ben-Shlomo said. “But the numbers continued to rise.”
He said the platform finished last year with close to NIS 400 million in donations, while the amount passing through JGive this year has already increased further.
“We saw a significant change in Israeli society’s attitude toward donations, solidarity, and the understanding that this is genuinely important for our resilience,” he said.
Israelis increasingly choose direct donations
Although Israel received substantial financial support from Jewish communities abroad following October 7, Ben-Shlomo said most of the money processed through JGive still comes from Israeli donors.
“It is true that during the war the balance changed and more money came from abroad, mainly from the United States,” he said. “But the bigger picture is that most still comes from Israel.”
The trend suggests that the post-October 7 solidarity story was not solely one of Diaspora Jews supporting Israel. Israelis themselves also increased their charitable giving.
At the same time, Ben-Shlomo said the war strengthened financial and emotional links between Israel and Jewish communities overseas, although those relationships have also become more complex.
One major change has been the rise of direct giving.
“In the past, central institutions and organizations had much more power,” he said. “Today, people like to give directly. If you want to donate to a specific nonprofit, you do not necessarily need an intermediary.”
Ben-Shlomo compared the shift to broader consumer behavior, in which people increasingly seek direct access instead of working through middlemen.
The change is particularly visible in the United States, he said, where donors can use digital tools to select a specific Israeli organization or project rather than automatically routing their contribution through established communal institutions.
“That does not mean the federations do not have a role,” he said. “They still have a very significant role, especially in philanthropy and large donations. But alongside that, there is now much more direct giving.”
Emergency fundraising gives way to rehabilitation
Immediately after October 7, JGive concentrated on helping nonprofits raise money as quickly as possible.
“When everything happened on that day, we understood that we needed to do two things,” Ben-Shlomo said. “One was to give nonprofits the time and tools and help them raise as much money as possible, as quickly as possible.”
The organization established an emergency operation to assist nonprofits using its platform. At the same time, JGive began receiving inquiries from donors around the world asking where their money was most urgently needed.
“We received calls from literally all over the globe asking, ‘How can we help?’” he said. “Then we understood there was a serious problem. Many donors simply did not know where to give. They wanted to donate, including companies, but they did not know where the money should go.”
That led to the creation of a national emergency fund intended to rapidly distribute money to organizations responding to needs on the ground.
“We were distributing money every evening,” Ben-Shlomo said. “Our approach was that the funds needed to reach many organizations because there were many needs.”
Nearly three years later, however, the definition of “need” has changed.
“At the beginning of the war, everyone stopped donating to routine causes, culture, education, health, everything that happens in ordinary life,” he said. “Almost everything stopped, and donations moved toward the emergency.”
Those initial needs were often basic, including food and assistance for evacuees. Over time, traditional areas of charitable giving began to recover, while an entirely new rehabilitation sector emerged around the consequences of October 7 and the war.
“There are many organizations that were established for needs created by October 7, and there is now an entire world moving toward rehabilitation,” Ben-Shlomo said.
Mental health, wounded soldiers drive new philanthropic needs
Ben-Shlomo said rehabilitation now includes wounded soldiers, mental-health care, civilian recovery, and long-term assistance for communities and families affected by the war.
“There are a great many needs,” he said. “There is the rehabilitation of soldiers, which is a very complicated event. There is mental health, and there is the civilian rehabilitation of many people following everything that happened.”
“The world of rehabilitation is a new chapter,” he added. “It is also bringing many good people into this field who were not part of it before.”
One notable development, he said, has been the arrival of professionals who previously had little involvement with nonprofits.
“You see organizations being established by doctors, psychologists, or other professionals who were not previously part of the nonprofit world,” he said. “It is very refreshing because people recognize a need and come with their professional expertise.”
The transition comes as Israel continues to face significant psychological consequences from the war, with health organizations reporting sustained demand for mental-health services.
Diaspora communities balance Israel support with needs at home
Ben-Shlomo described the relationship between Israel and Diaspora Jewry since October 7 as increasingly important but also increasingly complicated.
“I think it is a very complex situation,” he said. “The connection to Israel is more important than ever.”
He said rising antisemitism and security concerns around the world have strengthened some Diaspora Jews’ sense of connection to Israel.
“Because of everything happening around Jews in the world today, antisemitism and all of these terrible phenomena, it strengthens many people’s connection to Israel,” he said. “Israel is also a kind of more stable and secure anchor that they want to strengthen their connection with.”
At the same time, Jewish communities abroad are facing growing local expenses.
“Their local challenges are becoming more and more significant,” Ben-Shlomo said. “They need to invest more in protecting people, strengthening their own communities, and building resilience.”
“That makes philanthropy a more complicated issue,” he added. “But the willingness of Diaspora Jewry to create a strong connection with Israel and support important causes is still there.”
Younger donors want to know where their money goes
Donor behavior is also changing, Ben-Shlomo said, reflecting broader developments in philanthropy rather than October 7 alone.
“The new generation goes much further into the details and is interested in where its money goes,” he said. “It is not very different from the way people behave in the investment world.”
Donors increasingly expect transparency and want to understand how their money is being used.
October 7 accelerated that process by exposing many Israelis, particularly younger people, to nonprofits and volunteer activity for the first time.
“If, before October 7, we saw the world of donations as something that was nice to do, something reserved for a particular group, one of the changes we have undergone is that today everyone understands that it is essential and critical,” Ben-Shlomo said.
He recalled a conversation with a friend serving on the board of a business who described how social involvement had become part of professional identity.
Before board members even began discussing business, she told him, participants began describing the nonprofits where they volunteered or served in leadership positions.
“It naturally became a form of self-identity,” Ben-Shlomo said. “Many people feel they need to say that they are involved, whether through donations or volunteering.”
Nearly 90,000 donations in one holiday month
One figure that particularly surprised Ben-Shlomo was not a single major philanthropic contribution, but the sheer number of individual donors.
“In the last holiday month, there were almost 90,000 donations in one month, totaling NIS 60 million,” he said.
“That is one of the figures that always amazes me. It is not one major philanthropist giving a significant amount. It is a huge number of people donating, including small amounts.”
Many of JGive’s donors are young Israelis, he added.
“That really proves something about the Israeli DNA,” Ben-Shlomo said.
The larger question now is whether the solidarity that emerged after October 7 can be sustained during ordinary times.
“In an emergency, there is no question,” he said. “We saw that it happens.”
“The thing that concerns me more, and that we are working on a great deal, is how we take all the enthusiasm that existed during the emergency and turn it into something that happens in ordinary life,” he said. “That requires a great deal of work.”
Ben-Shlomo said the long-term goal should be to make social responsibility a permanent feature of Israeli life.
“I think our mission over the coming decades is to make Israel a social superpower as well,” he said. “There should truly be solidarity and a culture of mutual responsibility in which every person takes action, even if only in their own small area around their home, to look after the people there and those who need help.”

Time Magazine showcases prominent Jewish leaders in 'world's most influential rising stars' list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:36:00 UTC
06:36:00 KST

From artists and actors to technologists to politicians advancing visions for the future, Time Magazine has recognized Jewish figures on its list of “the world’s most influential rising stars.”
The magazine launched the Time100 Next list in 2019 to highlight people whose influence is still taking shape. This year’s list reflected shifts in popular culture, the AI revolution and responses to global crises from the United States to Israel.
Jewish members of Time100 Next have talked about their Jewishness as a source of inspiration, angst and activism. Here’s what nine have said about their Jewish identity.
Marisa Abela
Abela, an actress who rose to fame for her role in the TV financial drama series “Industry” and portrayed Amy Winehouse in the 2024 biopic “Back to Black,” grew up in England. She has described drawing from her mixed heritage to inhabit her characters.
“I am someone whose mum and dad come from completely different cultures, my dad is Maltese Arab, and my mum is from a family of Polish Jewish refugees,” Abela told The National in 2022.
While Abela’s background differs from that of her “Industry” character Yasmin Kara-Hanani, whose parents are Lebanese, she said that she understood the character’s family tensions. “The thing I relate to most is that those two cultures can be quite divisive, and you can feel like you’re being pulled in different directions,” she said.
To play Winehouse, Abela said she tapped into shared features of their early lives in Jewish households.
“The more I got to know her, the more I felt a major connection to this spiky Jewish girl from London who had a lot to say, and was really quite unafraid,” she told Harper’s Bazaar in a 2024 interview.
“I remembered how I felt when I was young, seeing that woman who was proud and cool, wearing a big Star of David in between a cleavage and a nice bra. I understood what a Friday-night dinner would look like in her home, the humor in her family.”
Jake Auchincloss
Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Auchincloss is one of his party’s staunchest advocates for centrism amid a rising wave of Democratic Socialists. He represents the state’s 4th Congressional District, spanning the heavily Jewish Boston suburbs of Brookline and Newton, where he grew up with a Jewish mother and Episcopalian father.
After a record of bolstering the Democrats’ pro-Israel wing in Congress, Auchincloss was among the majority of House Democrats who voted in July to cut $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Auchincloss argued the vote did not contradict his support for Israel. Instead, he said it was a vote against President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who he said had sacrificed the trust of Congress “with their disastrous war against Iran, their empowerment of settler violence in the West Bank, and their strategic incoherence against Islamist terrorism.”
He has also fended off progressive Democrats who denounce the United States-Israel alliance. In September, Auchincloss defeated a primary challenge from AI and policy researcher Jason Poulos, who said that he was animated by watching the United States send military aid to Israel and “participate actively in the genocide of the Palestinian people.”
Auchincloss told the Jerusalem News Syndicate in 2022 that “Judaism is important” to him even though he is “not a religious person.” He added that his parents’ interfaith marriage in the 1970s, which took place at the Harvard Memorial Church with a rabbi officiating, was “still a bit unusual” and made him more appreciative of his Jewish heritage as he was growing up.
Auchincloss has cited his family history as a factor in his decision to join the Marine Corps. In a 2021 interview with Roll Call, Auchincloss said his maternal grandfather enlisted in the Marines in 1942. Instead of deploying the 17-year-old in combat, the Marines sent him to study biomedical engineering at Purdue University, and he became a pioneer in artificial limbs.
“I just think about that, in one of the lowest moments of World War II, one of the lowest moments for Jews in our history, the U.S. government sent a Jewish kid in the Marine Corps to school,” said Auchincloss.
Molly Gordon
Actress and filmmaker Gordon has said that her Jewishness resonates throughout her career, not through observance, but through comedy.
Her Jewish roles span the 2020 comedy “Shiva Baby,” the 2023 mockumentary “Theater Camp,” which she also co-created, and the Hulu series “Ramy,” where she plays a Jewish woman who dates the title character, a Muslim. Gordon’s star has also risen through roles that are not identifiably Jewish, as in FX’s hit series “The Bear.”
“Being Jewish in West LA, my religion was watching comedy. That felt like God to me,” Gordon told Vulture in 2021.
The painter Sasha Gordon, who has no relation to Molly Gordon, won acclaim for her self-portraits set in surreal and nightmarish scenes. She has had multiple solo exhibitions in major cities, including “Haze” at the David Zwirner Gallery in New York City last year.
Gordon grew up in Somers, New York, with a Korean mother and a Polish American Jewish father. She told Vogue in 2023 that she and her brother were bullied in the predominantly white small town for being different.
“I don’t think I’m religious in any way, but I’d say that I’m culturally very Jewish,” said Gordon.
South African-born fashion designer Kallmeyer is the founder of Kallmeyer, a New York-based brand that specializes in suiting. She also became known for hosting pop-up Shabbat dinners that celebrated the Jewish queer community of New York.
In an interview with Gossamer, Kallmeyer described herself as a “gay Jewish business owner” with all the accompanying “anxiety.”
Joey King
King has been an actress since childhood, from the 2010 film “Ramona and Beezus” to the “Kissing Booth” series, which ran from 2018 to 2021, and the 2019 crime drama “The Act,” which won her an Emmy nomination. Her latest film, “Practical Magic 2,” premiered last month.
King opened up about her Jewish identity after starring in “We Were the Lucky Ones,” a 2024 Hulu miniseries based on a true story about Polish siblings who survived the Holocaust while scattered across the globe.
King told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in 2024 that she jumped at her first opportunity to play a Jewish woman.
“I couldn’t be prouder of who I am and my Jewish heritage,” said King. “When you get presented with a story like this, it’s just a once-in-a-lifetime feeling. It’s an immediate yes — to feel that you get to play a Jewish woman, and you are a Jewish woman.”
Naama Lazimi
Lazimi has been dubbed by Haaretz a “superstar” of the Israeli left. The lawmaker in Israel’s Knesset built her political profile with a focus on poverty and public housing, while protesting against Netanyahu’s government and calling for a state commission of inquiry into government failures surrounding the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
Lazimi said on social media that Time’s recognition came just before “the most important elections the State of Israel has ever known.” Lazimi’s Democrats Party hopes to join a centrist governing coalition after the Oct. 27 elections.
“This is not just a personal achievement, but a badge of honor for an entire camp in Israel, a glorious and determined camp that fights for the democratic character of our country, and for solidarity and social justice,” she said.
Lazimi is a longtime ally of Smol Emuni, or “Faithful Left,” a movement of religious left-wing Jews who advocate for peace and oppose the Gaza war. At a conference of Smol Emuni’s U.S. branch in New York, Lazimi said, “Peace is not just true security; it is also the most moral, and the most Jewish, choice.”
Yotam Segev
Israeli-born Segev is the leader of Cyera, a company that creates systems to defend sensitive data against attackers in the AI age. Founded in 2021, Cyera is now valued at $12 billion, according to Time.
Segev, who moved to New York four years ago, told CTech that he became more aware of being “a Jew in the U.S.” since the Gaza war. He cited rising incidents of antisemitism and the fear of being “perceived as someone’s enemy just because of where I come from.”
“When I walk around with my child, I don’t speak loudly in Hebrew without being aware of my surroundings,” said Segev.
Troye Sivan
Australian singer and actor Sivan went from performing the “shul circuit” as a child to Grammy-nominated pop stardom. He was raised in an Orthodox Jewish household. At 15, he came out after his father shared the belief that “it really doesn’t make sense” for religion to ban being gay, according to a 2019 interview with the New Yorker.
Sivan launched a lifestyle brand in 2023 called Tsu Lange Yor, the Yiddish phrase for “to long years.” He told W Magazine his great-grandmother spoke Yiddish at home when he was a child. While not himself “particularly religious,” Sivan said his Jewish identity formed a “huge part” of his cultural identity, and he continued to hold Shabbat dinners.
“Considering I’m not very religious and I’m queer, my Jewish identity was something I grappled with and was unsure about,” said Sivan. “I liked the idea of reclaiming it and proudly saying, even to other Jewish people, ‘I’m queer, and I’m also a Jew — and these are things that are both equally important in the makeup of who I am.’”

October 7 testimonies reach US audiences with new video archive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:35:39 UTC
06:35:39 KST

Friends of the Israel Defense Forces (FIDF) is launching a digital library of English-language video testimonies from soldiers, former hostages, bereaved families and others who experienced the Oct. 7 attacks and their aftermath, the organization said.
The archive, being launched ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks, is intended to make firsthand accounts accessible to FIDF donors and other supporters of Israel in the United States, including members of Jewish and Christian communities.
The library will initially include more than 50 filmed testimonies totaling over 12 hours of footage collected by FIDF. The organization said the archive will continue to expand as additional testimonies are recorded and added.
The project brings together accounts from IDF soldiers, lone soldiers, reservists, bereaved relatives, former hostages, community leaders and experts. The videos are divided into categories, allowing viewers to explore the events of Oct. 7 and the period that followed from different perspectives.
Among those featured are Moshe and Shira Shapira, the parents of Staff Sgt. Aner Shapira, who was killed during the attack; Rabbi Doron Perez, father of Capt. Daniel Perez, who was killed and whose body was taken to Gaza; and Col. Elad Edri, who recounts the attack on the IDF's Zikim base.
The archive also features Izzy Ezagui, an IDF veteran who lost an arm after being wounded during his military service and later returned to serve in the reserves.
Testimonies from former hostages include Noa Argamani, Amit Soussana, Maya Regev, Almog Meir Jan, Edan Alexander and Maxim Harkin.
FIDF said the initiative is intended both to preserve firsthand accounts for future generations and to give supporters abroad direct access to the people behind the events. The organization said the archive seeks to document stories of courage and resilience while helping communities outside Israel understand the personal experiences of those affected by the attacks and the war that followed.
"Since October 7, we have been moved by the surge of supporters across Jewish and Christian communities in the United States who want to understand more closely what happened in Israel on that devastating day and the days that followed and hear directly from the people who experienced it," said Maj. Gen. (res.) Nadav Padan, CEO of FIDF.
"Three years later, it is important not only to preserve these testimonies, but also to make them accessible in English to the communities that support Israel and IDF soldiers," Padan said. "This library allows them to hear firsthand from soldiers, hostage survivors and families, and to learn the personal stories behind October 7."

US Air Force removes all bombers from UK airbase targeted by suspected terror attack
Britain has linked last week’s incident to Tehran but Iran denies involvement. The move comes as Trump weighs options for his war on Iran
The US Air Force has removed its bombers stationed at a US-run military airbase in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday.
The move comes as US President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran – including new strikes – despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks.

Warnings ignored: Israel’s state watchdog struggles to make government act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:28:48 UTC
06:28:48 KST

Four days have passed since Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami tried to crash a flydubai flight bound for Israel, and the agencies responsible for background checks on foreign crew members flying into the country continued Sunday to shift responsibility among themselves.
In Israel in 2026, the pattern has become familiar: A failure occurs, only for it to emerge afterward that warnings had been issued that, had they been heeded, might have prevented it. In many cases, including the flydubai flight, those warnings came from the State Comptroller’s Office, a government watchdog whose standing has steadily eroded in recent years.
Under Israeli law, the state comptroller can issue recommendations but has no enforcement authority. In the past, however, comptroller reports commanded considerable respect both among the public and within government ministries. Politicization and a growing culture of evading responsibility and criticism have eroded that standing. Near the end of the previous Knesset’s term, there was even a controversial attempt to appoint Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s lawyer, Michael Rabello, to the position.
The post is currently vacant after the High Court of Justice ordered a new vote on the appointment. That dispute is only one example of the government’s relationship with the watchdog: A ynet review found that government ministries have failed to act on the comptroller’s recommendations in a range of areas in which deficiencies were identified.
‘A failure that cries out to the heavens’
Former state comptroller Matanyahu Englman warned as early as May 2024 of failures in the oversight and screening of aircrew members arriving in Israel. Although he recommended that the National Security Council conduct a comprehensive review together with the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Israel Airports Authority, Shin Bet domestic security agency and police, those recommendations appear not to have been implemented.
“Basically, the comptroller was right about everything he wrote, from A to Z,” said Danny Shenar, who headed the Transportation Ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division for 25 years.
“He says a state body needs to be established, that everything cannot rest with MAMLAT,” Shenar said, referring to the Aviation Security Operations Center, an operational body under the Transportation Ministry’s security division responsible for issuing security clearance for foreign flights seeking to land in Israel. “And that staff work needs to be done. It wasn’t done.”
Eyal Hulata, who headed the National Security Council under the government of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was equally critical.
“Nothing has been done since the comptroller’s report in 2024,” Hulata said. “It’s a failure that cries out to the heavens.”
Similar problems emerged in comptroller reports examining government failures in southern and northern Israel since 2023 and during the war.
A September 2025 report found that a forum of ministry directors-general held 27 meetings without making a single operational decision, that a civilian emergency command center was shut down within three months and that 43 emergency centers were operating without coordination.
A June 2025 report found that the evacuation of 43 communities along Israel’s northern border was carried out without coordination among government ministries. In February 2026, the comptroller found that the evacuation of 210,000 residents was marred by systemic failures and that billions of shekels transferred to hotels were not adequately monitored.
Engelman has also said the 2021 Mount Meron disaster could have been prevented. In 2008, about 13 years before 45 people were killed in a crush during the annual Lag BaOmer pilgrimage at the tomb of second-century Jewish sage Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai, the State Comptroller’s Office had already published a report detailing safety deficiencies at the site and problems with preparations for the event. The disaster was Israel’s deadliest civilian catastrophe before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
The warnings have extended beyond civilian matters.
In December, Englman published his annual security report, which he said “should keep government ministers awake at night.”
The report identified “a series of deficiencies” across a range of security-related areas, including preparedness for a terrorist attack on the Tel Aviv metropolitan area’s light rail system, security at Ramon International Airport in southern Israel and follow-up work on protecting critical infrastructure against missiles, rockets and other aerial threats.
It also examined the employment of consultants by the Defense Ministry, the ministry’s oversight of defense companies’ use of marketing agents and intermediaries in defense export deals, measures to prevent biological pathogens and knowledge that could be used to develop biological weapons from leaking and the management and security of Defense Ministry databases.
A coordinator is no magic solution
Following the flydubai incident, officials are again calling for the appointment of a special coordinator and a central body to oversee the issue.
Einav Peretz, an accountant and expert on governance and auditing who formerly chaired the association of municipal auditors and now heads the National Center for Municipal Knowledge and Management, told ynet that appointing a coordinator is not a cure-all.
“We need to be careful and not say about everything, ‘We need a coordinating body here,’” she said. “There is a chain of activity, and you have to decide which government ministry leads the response. If it’s the Transportation Ministry, then the entire chain of events needs to be under it, and someone needs to manage it.”
Peretz said a distinction must be made between a prolonged, government-wide crisis and a failure to enforce procedures that already exist.
“You have to separate when a coordinator is needed, when the issue is acute and ongoing, from when there is a procedure that isn’t being followed — in which case it needs to be followed and one body needs to be responsible for it,” she said.
“I don’t think there was any lack of clarity in the flydubai case over who does what. There were procedures there. They simply weren’t followed. The gap here is between a clear procedure and its actual implementation. There is a procedure, and it is clear: Pilots must not hold citizenship from an enemy state.”
For broader, persistent problems, such as crime in the Arab sector or the rehabilitation of communities in the north and south, Peretz said a coordinating body under the Prime Minister’s Office is necessary — but only if it has the authority to act.
“Otherwise, every ministry will continue working on its own,” she said.
Peretz also pointed to the limited impact of audit reports when their findings are not implemented.
“Their success will be measured when they are implemented,” she said. “It depends on the comptroller, how personal the conclusions are, how the deficiencies are followed up and what happens if they aren’t corrected.”
“An audit report is the beginning of the correction process,” she added. “To complete it, you need a responsible body, deadlines, follow-up and consequences for failing to correct the deficiencies. There also needs to be an enforcement mechanism for state comptroller reports.”
No enforcement powers — and no comptroller
The State Comptroller’s Office, which Englman headed until July and which has remained without a permanent leader amid controversy over the process to choose his successor, operates within legal limits that prevent it from enforcing its recommendations. It can identify shortcomings and warn of the dangers they pose, but it cannot compel government bodies to fix them.
The agencies and ministries it audits are legally required to submit plans for correcting deficiencies. Oversight of whether those plans are implemented, however, rests with the Knesset, primarily through its State Control Committee, which can summon officials to account for their actions. Media coverage and the resulting public scrutiny can also help pressure agencies to implement recommendations.
In other words, Israeli law deliberately established the state comptroller as a watchdog and advisory authority, not an enforcement body.
Although government agencies are sometimes portrayed as completely ignoring the comptroller’s recommendations, that is not entirely accurate. Agencies do implement recommendations and correct deficiencies, though not all of them.
About 20% of the reports issued by the State Comptroller’s Office each year are follow-up audits, in which investigators revisit previously examined issues to assess what has changed. Those reports also identify deficiencies that have been corrected.
In June, the Knesset held a vote to choose Englman’s successor between Rabello, Netanyahu’s attorney, and retired Supreme Court Justice Yosef Elron.
A month later, High Court justices invalidated the process, ruling that it had been fundamentally flawed and ordering another vote. That vote has yet to take place.
The decision came after several lawmakers photographed themselves casting ballots for Rabello even though the vote is required by law to be secret.
A growing workload
The State Comptroller’s Office does not focus only on national security.
The Oct. 7 massacre and its effects on Israeli society underscored the importance of the country’s social welfare services both during emergencies and in everyday life.
In addition to routine responsibilities such as assisting families of children with special needs, at-risk youth, older people and families facing financial hardship, social workers have been tasked with supporting bereaved families, evacuees, military reservists and people affected by the war.
At the same time, conditions in municipal social services departments have continued to deteriorate. The Welfare Ministry and local governments have struggled to fill positions, leaving social workers with growing caseloads.
In 2021, the Welfare Ministry published an internal report examining difficulties in recruiting social workers for municipal welfare departments. But a recent state comptroller report found that the ministry had not prepared an overall budget estimate detailing the cost of fully implementing the report’s recommendations.
Another unresolved issue is workload. The ministry has not established a maximum number of cases that an individual social worker should handle, leaving caseloads to continue growing.
“Although the Welfare Ministry was aware of social workers’ workloads, it has not yet completed development of a new formula” used to determine the number of positions funded in each municipality, the comptroller said in a June 2026 report.
That remained the case “even though two years have already passed since the outbreak of the war, which exacerbated the manpower shortage in municipal social services departments,” the report said.
A year and a half to see a psychologist
The war has also presented the health system with unprecedented challenges, including treating large numbers of wounded people, coping with surging demand for mental health care and addressing inadequate protection at hospitals against missiles and other attacks.
As early as November 2023, the state comptroller warned of gaps discovered during visits to communities near Israel’s borders. Among them were shortcomings in protected spaces at some hospitals that required immediate attention, particularly in rooms where lifesaving treatment is provided.
A state comptroller report published in early 2026 examining hospital protection between January and September 2024 found serious deficiencies that remained far from resolved.
About 56% of hospital beds at the 27 general hospitals examined — roughly 10,500 of 18,900 — lacked adequate protection. About 41% of operating rooms, 168 of 406, were also unprotected. The audit found that a significant proportion of medical imaging equipment and catheterization rooms were similarly unprotected.
In long-term care facilities, including geriatric, psychiatric and rehabilitation hospitals in the Health Ministry’s Dan district in central Israel, about 93% of beds lacked adequate protection, including beds located in areas classified as the “most protected available.” That amounted to 1,860 of 2,000 beds.
The war also exposed longstanding shortcomings in Israel’s mental health system, which had faced chronic funding and staffing shortages even before Oct. 7.
A sharply critical state comptroller report published in February 2025 painted a bleak picture of the mental health response available to Israelis following the Oct. 7 attack and during the war.
Even now, despite expanded services through health maintenance organizations, progress on the Health Ministry’s national mental health program — budgeted at 1.4 billion shekels — and new wage agreements in the system, patients seeking psychologists or psychiatrists through the public health system continue to face extremely long waits.
A November 2025 survey by the Forum of Organizations for Public Psychology found that waiting times for publicly funded psychological treatment averaged as long as 18 months.
Short on protection, short on equipment
In December 2025, the state comptroller published a report on shelters and protective infrastructure in Israeli municipalities, warning that about 25% of students — roughly half a million children and teenagers — lacked adequate protected spaces at their schools. As a result, many would be unable to attend school during wartime.
A survey of school principals conducted by the State Comptroller’s Office found that at 39% of schools, not all students could reach protected spaces within the required warning time.
The Knesset Education Committee and State Control Committee held hearings on the findings. The report found that 14% of educational institutions had no protective infrastructure at all, 24% had partial protection, 24% had protection meeting the required standard and 38% had protection exceeding the standard.
In another audit, the comptroller examined the psychological toll of the war on students.
Rates of emotional distress among children were already high before Oct. 7, with 61% of parents reporting that their children experienced difficulties between 2018 and 2023.
The comptroller found that about 53% of middle and high school students experienced psychosomatic symptoms at the beginning of the war. Yet most parents whose children were struggling did not seek help from local educational psychology services, which operate in schools and kindergartens, because they were unaware the services existed. The gap was particularly pronounced among Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish families.
The comptroller also warned that the Education Ministry had not updated for more than 35 years the formula governing the ratio of educational psychologists employed by local authorities to the number of students they serve.
As a result, children face waits of about 55 days for educational psychology services, while parents who need urgent appointments are often forced to pay for private treatment.
A separate audit found that despite recommendations in a 2021 state comptroller report and an Education Ministry strategic process conducted in 2021 and 2022, schools remained inadequately equipped for digital learning in both routine periods and emergencies.
An Education Ministry technology survey conducted in early 2023 found that about 23% of responding schools had a low level of digital equipment and about 66% had a medium level.
Surveys of principals and parents conducted by the State Comptroller’s Office found that significant shortages of equipment for remote teaching and learning persisted during the war, particularly among students, affecting about 72% of schools, but also among teachers, affecting about 48%.
The shortages reduced schools’ ability to conduct remote learning and undermined its effectiveness. Among principals whose schools did not conduct remote learning during the emergency, 27% cited the lack of equipment as one of the main reasons.

Key Event
The deals that have already been done
While the trade period only officially opened today, the free agency period actually began on Friday, so free agents have been able to move clubs since then.
In those three days, we saw a handful of players switch clubs. It just so happens that some of those players were genuine stars of the game. Here's what you might have missed:
- Lachie Neale to Collingwood (Lions receive band three compensation)
- Toby Greene to Geelong (Giants receive band three compensation)
- Joel Amartey to Carlton (Swans receive band three compensation)
- Jordon Butts to Western Bulldogs (Crows receive band three compensation)
- Kieren Briggs to Richmond (Giants receive band four compensation)
Not a bad start to the window.
If you're wondering, "band three compensation" means a draft pick after the club's natural second round pick. So the Giants got pick 26 for Greene, the Swans pick 37 for Amartey etc. Band four is the same thing, but in the third round of draft picks.
There was some surprise and disappointment from the Giants, Lions and Crows in the outcome as each were hoping for a band two compensation pick (which would have come at the end of the first round). Seems to me the AFL is trying to water down free agency compensation a little this year.

US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot

Unknown Publisher

The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”
At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.
There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.
According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.
A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.
“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.
The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

The Taliban movement, which controls Afghanistan, has begun purchasing weapons and drones from Belarus. Details

At the same time, Minsk has recently been expanding contacts with the Taliban. In August, a delegation of 13 representatives of the movement visited Belarus, and the Taliban also approved the candidacy of a Belarusian ambassador on a non-resident basis.

US removes B-1 bombers from UK base amid security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:23:41 UTC
06:23:41 KST

US rushes to withdraw bombers from UK air base after new threats
Eric Schmitt
WASHINGTON – The United States rushed over the weekend to withdraw all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from an airbase in southern England after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation, two US officials said on Oct 4.
The withdrawal was highly unusual. Such moves are rarely made so quickly from an allied airbase in a peacetime country thousands of kilometres from a combat zone.
The need to move the bombers out of the base, RAF Fairford, was deemed so urgent that some of the planes and their flight crews left while aerial refueling aircraft were still being scrambled to support their flights to the United States. 
At least three of the planes had landed at their home base in South Dakota by Oct 4, the officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.
The Pentagon’s European Command confirmed on Oct 4 that the bombers had left England but declined to comment on any new warnings.
“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford are redeploying to their home stations in the United States,” the command said in a statement. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.”
The British Ministry of Defence declined to comment on the movements of US military assets.
US officials on Oct 4 declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces. 
One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.
The sudden pullout of the bombers came a week after the British police arrested five men who had been travelling on Sept 27 in white vans near the base, which has been used by US bombers in the US-Israeli war against Iran. The men were released on bail a day later after the authorities did not discover explosives in the vans.
But the police have repeatedly said the men remain under investigation, and a dual British-Iranian national was arrested on Oct 1 on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that the British government believed Iran played a part in planning those events. US and British officials, as well as those in Germany and Israel, believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Iran has denied the accusations.
The episode has presented the authorities with myriad puzzles as they try to sort out the events over the past week, including the arrests, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives and a national security meeting convened by Burnham.
In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for US actions. “Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory”, the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces”.
In September, US military commanders received a chilling warning from US and other Western intelligence agencies, according to US officials briefed on the information: RAF Fairford was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.
The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.
After that initial warning in September, concern among officials across Europe surged. According to a senior US official, Israel warned Germany that US bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.
An Iran-backed plot to commit an attack in Britain would be a major escalation by Tehran against a Western country in apparent retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Iran. NYTIMES
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Brazil election: Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of populist Jair Bolsonaro, takes an early lead over rival Lula da Silva with over 30% of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:19:00 UTC
06:19:00 KST

With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.
With nearly 91% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 48% of the vote. Lula has just over 44%, according to the electoral court.
Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo.
Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing.
You can watch our live coverage of the Brazil election results on YouTube or in the livestream window above this article.
Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.
Bolsonaro calls for 'change'
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.
The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch
The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.
Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."
What happens next?
Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.
In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

The European Union and Canada plan to announce a new broad strategic partnership covering defense, energy, technology, critical raw materials and continued support for Ukraine. The agreement is expected to be presented at a summit in Montreal, which will begin on October 29, Politico reports, citing a draft joint statement, writes UNN.
Details
The document states that the EU and Canada seek to significantly deepen their economic and strategic ties amid global geopolitical and trade changes.
The parties plan to accelerate investment in the extraction of critical minerals, strengthen supply chains and create strategic raw material stockpiles to reduce dependence on external markets.
Defense, Ukraine and the Arctic
One of the key areas of the new partnership will be the integration of Canada’s and the EU’s defense industries. The parties are also expected to deepen cooperation in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and quantum technologies, and make the Arctic one of their joint strategic projects.
A separate element of the future partnership will be continued joint support for Ukraine.
The EU and Canada also plan to develop cooperation in the energy sector — from liquefied natural gas and nuclear power to hydropower, solar and wind generation.
In addition, Ottawa and Brussels are preparing the joint purchase of 50 De Havilland aircraft to fight wildfires. They are expected to be ready for use in Canada and Europe in 2030.
