====================================================================================================

What to look for during the AFL trade period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:13:14 UTC
06:13:14 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Footy never truly sleeps. Just days after the final siren sounded in one of the most chaotic AFL grand finals in memory did the competition begin once again.
The trade period can help sides find the missing pieces in their side, while the draft provides young footballers the opportunity to play on the biggest of stages.
Seventeen clubs are looking to catch the reigning premiers, while Brisbane is doing its best to stay ahead of the pack. No games are won during the off-season, but a good period can set sides up for years to come.
The names of countless players and draft picks have been discussed by the list managers in earnest over the last year, all ahead of the two weeks to come. These are the key themes to watch out for as the AFL enters its silly season.
A star-studded crop
This time of year lives and dies on the star power of the names linked to new clubs. If the trade period is about hope, then only the best in the game truly drives that optimism.
On achievements alone you would be hard pressed to find a trade period where more highly credentialed players have found new clubs.
Already a two-time Brownlow Medallist with three flags, Lachie Neale has found his way to his third club, Collingwood. He's set to replace AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury in the Pies midfield. Pendlebury is set to finish his career like many future Victorian retirees do; on the sunny sands of the Gold Coast.
Elsewhere, GWS games and goals record holder Toby Greene has found his way to Geelong, and fellow former GWS teammate and Coleman medallist Jesse Hogan is set to join his fourth club, Collingwood. These players are joined by several others who have achieved plenty across their careers already.
But despite the list of greats looking for another club, one younger star has grabbed the lion's share of the headlines. Unlike the names listed above, Zak Butters, firmly in his prime and off a top 10 finish in the Brownlow Medal, is poised to move east if Port declines to match a contract offer from the Western Bulldogs.
Butters will attract top Band 1 compensation, but other high-profile moves have not. Compensation is tied to last year's salaries of players across the league. The sharp jump in the total player payment cap in recent years saw inflated compensation as a result.
Those effects have now dissipated, with the likes of Lachie Neale and Toby Greene attracting lower compensation picks than they may have a year or two ago.
These stars are far from the only players that will be discussed heavily over the coming 10 days. It's expected up to 40 trades involving about 30 players will be made during the player movement period, with many negotiations already firmly underway.
Beyond the list of vested greats, there's an uptick in the number of rucks and key position players expected to find new homes. As the league trends back towards multiple key forwards and an extended bench, clubs lacking depth are searching for answers.
No surprise about number one
In many — if not most — years there's intrigue about who is likely to be the number one pick in the November draft. Recruiters and scouts alike are scouring over player videos and stat profiles, trying to separate the wheat from the chaff.
But not so much in 2026.
Thanks to a recent rule change from the AFL, Essendon are heavily incentivised to pick a player tied to a club via the father-son or academy rules. If it does, it'll give itself (plus up to four other clubs) an extra high-end draft pick.
"We're certainly planning for Dougie to be bid on at one," Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps told Trade Radio last week.
"I'm happy to share that Essendon has told us that as well."
This year that player is almost certain to be Dougie Cochrane. The young key position player from South Australia is the son of former Port player Stuart, and brother of current Port midfielder Tom.
However, Dougie isn't eligible for the father-son process, and is instead tied to Port via its Next Generation Academy (NGA). He is set to become the second NGA player to be chosen at pick one after Jamarra Ugle-Hagan.
Cochrane has missed almost the entire year with injury, but his 2025 junior season was incredibly impressive. If there was a fully open draft there may be questions about whether he would go first, but under the current rules there's little doubt.
The new rule seeks to better aid lowly clubs seen as missing out on top talent and it may also address some reluctance by clubs with early picks to actually bid on high-value tied players.
The new scheme is a de facto priority pick system for bottom five clubs. With the introduction of Tasmania and years of compromised drafts ahead (more on that later), this could be a handy leg-up to strugglers. This bonus draft pick disappears if the original is traded, so only lopsided trade offers are likely to be entertained.
A bleak draft future?
Last week the Tasmania Football Club unveiled its first eight players to the football world. For many list managers it acted as an alarm that tough times were coming on the draft front.
Each club values the crop of each draft in different ways. Some drafts have stronger top ends, but weak depth. Others are even throughout. While last year's draft fell away sharply after the early picks, this year is considered to be deeper throughout the pack.
That's a key reason that this year's picks are being considered to hold a premium on their usual value, but it's not the only one. This year's draft will be the last majorly uncompromised for at least two seasons. This is due to the list concessions awarded to Tasmania on entry to the competition.
"We've obviously got Tasmania coming in who are going to dominate the next three drafts." Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told Melbourne Media last week.
Like GWS and the Suns on their entry to the league, the Devils have been awarded a generous set of list-building tools to construct their first side. These include access to elite players in their pre-draft year, $5m in signing bonuses to established players, extra draft picks to both use and on-trade, and mini-draft picks to auction off. All in all, as few as nine of the top 25 players in next year's draft will be untouched by Tasmania's entry.
That's before considering the expected strong crop of both father-son and academy talents across the next two drafts, including some available to Tasmania under its academy, structured like those in NSW and Queensland.
As a result, many clubs are looking to prioritise picking up talent in this year's draft unless they have academy or father-son talent in the coming two years. It could mean that the value of future draft picks is significantly lower than in previous years, with clubs struggling to see eye to eye on what's fair.
With a strong crop of draft talent this year (even after excluding tied players), teams may spend relatively large amounts to secure any available picks for this draft. These factors, when combined, might make trading for talents such as Zach Merrett and Rowan Marshall even harder than in years' past.

Feature: A home in ashes, a livelihood lost amid settler attacks in West Bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:11:36 CST
06:11:36 KST

RAMALLAH, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- With a pale face and eyes heavy with sorrow, 60-year-old Mahmoud Tubasi stands every day on the roof of his father's house in Jalud village, northern West Bank, gazing at his two burned homes from afar.
The houses, once clad in Jerusalem stone, a natural white limestone widely used in Palestinian construction, are now blackened by fire -- scars that will never fade from his and his wife's hearts.
"My wife's condition is very bad. She has suffered a mental breakdown and has hallucinations every day," Tubasi said. After a long pause, he added that he himself had lately been having nightmares of settlers attacking him.
The nightmare began when he tried to return home a few days ago.
On Sept. 29, Tubasi and his family, escorted by the Israeli army, returned to their home south of Jalud after more than 70 days away. Before the soldiers left, settlers arrived -- and set their home on fire.
The army put Tubasi and his wife in a jeep and drove them to a spot 100 meters away.
Speaking of the fire, Tubasi stared at the ground, his voice low: "My wife was crying beside me. I felt something stuck in my chest. I jumped out of the car window to stop this madness, but the Israeli army took us away from the scene."
Tubasi's family had built their home brick by brick over three years, at a cost of about 500,000 new shekels (about 163,500 U.S. dollars).
Recalling their past life, a fleeting smile crossed his face. "The air was fresh, and we could see the mountains in Jordan and, on clear days, Jericho," he said. "Our family was once the envy of the village."
"But in July this year, settlers occupied my house. I squeezed into my father's two-story house with my wife and daughter, and my two sons were forced to move away -- one to Ramallah and the other to Kafr Yasif," Tubasi said, his eyes brimming with tears.
Tubasi later saw photos of his burned home: settlers had placed tires inside to start the fire, burning the house to the ground and leaving behind only a scarred shell.
In the West Bank, settler violence has intensified. UN data shows that in 2026 alone, about 3,800 Palestinians have been displaced by settler violence, house demolitions and evictions. More than 1,430 incidents involving Israeli settlers have been recorded this year, affecting about 260 Palestinian communities.
Tubasi lost not only his property but also about 26 dunams (about 2.6 hectares) of land -- his only source of income. "The harvest season is approaching, and the trees are full of olives, but no one dares to pick them."
"I planted about 350 olive trees. Settlers cut down more than half of them, chopped down the fig and apricot trees, and uprooted the grapevines. Even the metal fence and gate I installed in the orchard were dismantled. Nothing was left," he said.
Jalud village, located southwest of Nablus with an area of only 1,580 hectares, is almost surrounded by settlements and outposts. Tubasi's home faces a newly built settlement across a valley, at a straight-line distance of only about one kilometer.
Tubasi said Jalud had enjoyed relative calm despite nearby settlements until January, when an outpost known as Ras al-Ain appeared. A road linking the outpost to a nearby settlement runs past his home, and harassment intensified afterward.
Data from the Palestinian official body, the Wall and Settlement Resistance Committee, shows that Nablus Governorate recorded 900 settler attacks in the first half of 2026, the highest among West Bank governorates; in August alone, the governorate saw 137 attacks.
"This is not just about the house. They want to seize the whole land. They do not recognize us as the legal owners and believe the land belongs to them," Tubasi added. ■

In the first three days of the holiday from Oct. 1 to 3, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively.
Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 19.63 billion yuan (about 2.91 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 3.48 million consumers.
In breakdown, the program drove trade-ins of 46,000 vehicles, generating 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales, along with 1.51 million home appliances worth 6.5 billion yuan and 1.71 million digital and smart devices worth 4.9 billion yuan.
The National Day holiday has long been one of China's peak periods for travel, tourism and spending. Authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips in total over the seven days, averaging 300 million a day.
Previous data have suggested demand remains strong as railway passenger trips on Oct. 1 alone reached 25.2 million, a single-day record.
To meet surging demand, China has added train services on busy routes and waived highway tolls for private cars during the holiday.
Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign in late September.
Local governments are hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, while also handing out some 310 million yuan in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption. ■

====================================================================================================

News Analysis: Chinese partnership helps Spain strengthen EV value chain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:11:10 CST
06:11:10 KST

MADRID, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Spain builds more than 2 million vehicles a year as Europe's second-largest vehicle producer, but many decisions shaping its automotive industry are made abroad. With Volkswagen considering a possible phase-out of its Spanish brand SEAT after 2030, a new battery partnership with China's Gotion High-Tech highlights Spain's efforts to secure its place in the electric-vehicle value chain.
Volkswagen Group, its battery unit PowerCo and Gotion announced on Sept. 28 that Gotion will invest around 1.1 billion euros (1.29 billion U.S. dollars) for a 49-percent stake in PowerCo's battery-cell plant in Sagunto, eastern Spain. PowerCo will retain 51 percent, with the venture intended to be jointly managed and operations to start in 2027.
Jose Diez, second vice president of the Valencian regional government, said the partnership would combine "industrial experience and technological knowledge" to make the project more competitive.
A POWERHOUSE WITH LIMITED CONTROL
Spain has an extensive automotive manufacturing ecosystem spanning assembly plants, component makers and supplier network. According to ICEX, Spain's state export and investment agency, nine multinational groups operate 18 vehicle assembly and component plants in the country. The broader automotive industry accounts for around 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and 16 percent of goods exports.
Yet much of that industrial strength sits within multinational groups, leaving Spain exposed to investment and production decisions made elsewhere.
Uncertainty over SEAT has brought that vulnerability into focus. In September, Volkswagen said tighter CO2 rules, electrification costs and the investment needed for a new generation of electric models were making further investment in the brand increasingly complex. Volkswagen's options beyond 2030 include a gradual phase-out.
The announcement has stirred concerns in Spain. El Pais reported that SEAT's direct and indirect economic footprint is estimated at around 4 percent of Catalonia's GDP and 3 percent of employment.
Matias Carnero, president of SEAT's works council and currently a member of Volkswagen's supervisory board, has warned against allowing SEAT to become "a mere assembly plant." He told Catalan newspaper La Vanguardia that SEAT still retains activities spanning design, production and sales. "The whole value chain - that is what matters," he said.
WHY CHINESE TECHNOLOGY MATTERS
Electrification is changing what gives automotive manufacturers a competitive edge.
"It is no longer just about who manufactures better, but who controls batteries, software, costs and the speed of innovation," Xavier Ferre, partner responsible for automotive and transport at EY Spain, told local media La Vanguardia.
Batteries illustrate that shift. According to Volkswagen, Europe still lacks significant industrial-scale production capacity for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, a technology increasingly used in lower-cost mass-market electric vehicles. Gotion brings established expertise in LFP technology and large-scale manufacturing.
The new partnership aims to make Sagunto a European production hub for LFP-based Unified Cells. The plant's first phase is now planned at up to 30 GWh of annual capacity, 50 percent above the 20 GWh initially considered.
The cells are intended to feed Volkswagen Group's electric-vehicle production network in Spain, including small electric models assembled at SEAT's Martorell plant in Catalonia and Volkswagen Navarra.
Another major project is taking shape in Zaragoza, where Stellantis and China's CATL are investing up to 4.1 billion euros (4.62 billion dollars) in a 50-50 joint venture to build an LFP battery plant with a capacity of up to 50 GWh. Construction began in 2025, and production is scheduled to start by the end of 2026.
Such projects could help Spain anchor battery manufacturing alongside vehicle assembly, strengthening its position as production shifts toward electric models.
FROM COMPETITION TO INDUSTRIAL COOPERATION
Spain's partnerships with Chinese companies extend beyond batteries. Chery has partnered with Spanish brand Ebro to revive production at Nissan's former Barcelona plant. Ford and Geely have agreed to form a joint venture around the Almussafes plant in Valencia, pending regulatory approval. Stellantis is also deepening industrial cooperation with Leapmotor, with production planned in Zaragoza.
These alliances offer ways to sustain factories and supplier networks while attracting new technology and investment.
Battery investment is pushing localization further upstream. Gotion's separate project in Valladolid includes cathode production and advanced battery recycling, adding activities beyond vehicle assembly. When the project was announced in July, the Spanish government described it as a "historic opportunity" to strengthen the country's electric-vehicle industrial base, with thousands of jobs expected to be created.
Josep Maria Vall, president of the Catalan Automotive Industry Cluster (CIAC), said Spain's manufacturing history and experienced component makers give it the capacity to integrate Chinese manufacturers into its industrial ecosystem. CIAC Manager Josep Nadal said deeper investment and industrial alliances could help Europe "retain the value chain."
Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, told Xinhua that Chinese brands are pushing European companies to improve quality, accelerate innovation and increase efficiency. "Spain and Europe need Chinese brands to accelerate innovation," he said.
Jaume Roura, president of Catalonia's Fecavem vehicle dealers' association, told Xinhua that cooperation should deliver benefits on both sides. "We must make sure everyone benefits and, above all, that industry and jobs are maintained," he said. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- As the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) accelerates its advance across the country's conflict-hit Tigray region, concerns are mounting over the conflict's potential regional spillover amid heightened diplomatic tensions.

These efforts will enable the people of Tigray to govern themselves, restore peace and stability to the region, while paving the way for regional elections "within a few months," ENA quoted Abraham Belay, former head of the federally appointed interim administration in Tigray, as saying.
Belay said that following these operations, new administrative structures will be established from the lower locality levels upward with direct community participation. He called on all Ethiopians to support the ongoing efforts to conclude the transitional phase and allow the people of Tigray to fully participate in national development.
FEDERAL FORCES' CONTINUED ADVANCE
Local residents who spoke to Xinhua on Sunday confirmed that the Ethiopian army and its allied forces, mainly the Tigray Peace Force, took control of Mekelle, the Tigray regional state capital, late Saturday afternoon.
Amid the continued military operations, reports and video clips posted on social media on Sunday also indicated that federal troops have continued pushing further into northern Tigray.
Experts and political analysts said the ENDF's control of Mekelle marks a new phase in the continued military escalation in northern Ethiopia, following the Sept. 20 announcement of a new alliance formed by seven Ethiopian opposition and armed groups.
Despite large-scale military confrontations during the earlier days of this latest round of conflict, mainly in parts of southern Tigray, reports indicated that federal forces took control of the regional capital with limited fighting in or around the city.
In a video message released Thursday, TPLF Chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael indicated that his forces were in a defensive mode and would engage in guerrilla-style attacks as the conflict progresses.
Recent developments have raised concerns about a possible relapse into full-blown war, set against the backdrop of the devastating two-year conflict between federal forces and TPLF-loyal troops from November 2020 to November 2022. That previous conflict left millions in urgent need of humanitarian assistance before the two parties signed the landmark Pretoria peace accord in South Africa to end hostilities.
REGIONAL SPILLOVER CONCERNS
As military tensions continue in northern Ethiopia, the situation has raised growing concerns over the conflict's potential regional spillover. Recent developments have also ignited heightened diplomatic tensions, primarily among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt.
In an interview with the state news agency, Belay noted that both internal and external actors are "attempting to destabilize Ethiopia." He specifically accused Ethiopia's northern neighbor, Eritrea, claiming that its forces "had participated in the conflict alongside the TPLF and other groups," which he characterized as "anti-peace forces."
Amid escalating diplomatic rifts, Ethiopia announced Thursday the closure of its embassy in Asmara, the Eritrean capital, in response to what it calls "Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
In a direct response, Eritrea announced the complete severance of ties with Ethiopia, marking a total breakdown in relations between the two Horn of Africa neighbors. Rejecting Addis Ababa's allegations, the Eritrean government accused Ethiopia of "pursuing an agenda of incessant hostility."
Also on Thursday, the Ethiopian government declared a diplomatic staff member at the Egyptian Embassy in Addis Ababa persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours. In a reciprocal move, Cairo declared a counselor at the Ethiopian Embassy in Egypt persona non grata, also ordering him to leave within 48 hours.
Ethiopian analysts attribute the latest diplomatic tensions among the three African nations to the ongoing military escalation in northern Ethiopia.
In light of the deteriorating diplomatic relations among the three countries, the African Union has called on the three member states to exercise "maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability." ■

SARAJEVO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Denis Becirovic, Zeljka Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic led the race for seats in Bosnia and Herzegovina's (BiH's) tripartite presidency, according to preliminary results released Sunday by the Central Election Commission.
The results were based on ballots from about 92 percent of the polling stations.
Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party of BiH (SDP) led the race for the Bosniak seat. Born in Tuzla in 1975, he has served in cantonal and federal parliaments and completed three terms as a member of the Parliamentary Assembly.
Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the race for the Serb seat. Born in Teslic in 1967, she previously held government positions in Republika Srpska, mainly in international cooperation and European integration.
Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union of BiH (HDZ BiH) led the race for the Croat seat in her first presidential bid. Born in Mostar in 1987, she is party vice president and a member of the national parliament's House of Representatives.
Under the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, BiH consists of two entities: the Federation of BiH and Republika Srpska. General elections are held every four years. According to the country's electoral system, voters in the Federation of BiH elect the Bosniak and Croat members of the presidency, while voters in Republika Srpska elect the Serb member. All three serve four-year terms.
The 2026 elections are the ninth general elections held in BiH since 1996, when the Dayton Peace Agreement ended the 1992-1995 war and established the country's post-war constitutional order. ■

Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:00:38 UTC
06:00:38 KST

The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency.
The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding.
The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls.
Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK.
Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.”
“Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.”
In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready.
The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say.
The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”.
Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments.
Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”.
In his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.
“Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.”
Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours, has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say.
Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously.

‘Anyone seeking to lead has to provide full and honest answers,’ Eisenkot challenges Netanyahu inviting him to an election debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:56:30 UTC
05:56:30 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel elections 2026
- Gadi Eisenkot challenges Netanyahu to televised debate ahead of Israel election
Gadi Eisenkot challenges Netanyahu to televised debate ahead of Israel election
Eisenkot's party said it was ready to hold the debate immediately under those terms, claling for talks to coordinate the details as soon as possible
Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot formally invited Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take part in a televised debate ahead of Israel's election at the end of this month.
The invitation, issued on the eve of the national memorial day marking the October 7 massacre, called for a "direct, public debate" broadcast live across Israeli media.
"In 23 days, Israel will hold its most fateful elections, standing at a critical crossroads regarding the security and future of the State of Israel," the party said.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of refusing to establish a commission of inquiry into the October 7 failures and of refusing to release full transcripts related to the events.
"Anyone seeking to lead has a duty to provide full, direct, and honest answers to the voters," Eisenkot said. "They deserve clear and complete answers, free from spin and lies."
Yashar laid out three main principals for the debate:
- A format will be established that allows for substantive and comprehensive answers, and enables all Israeli media outlets to broadcast it.
- The debate moderators will be journalists selected by news channel editors.
- The rules of the debate and discussion, including time allocation, the questioning format, and other details, will be determined through coordination between the selected moderators and representatives of the candidates' campaign teams.
Eisenkot's party said it was ready to hold the debate immediately under those terms and called for talks to coordinate the details as soon as possible.
Why doesn't Israel hold many electoral debates?
Unlike many other democracies Israel does not have a strong tradition of public electoral debates. Public televised electoral debates first began in 1977 when Likud's Menachem Begin and Labor's Shimon Peres held a debate patterned on US presidential debates.
Debates between Labor and Likud continued well into the 1990s. The 1996 debate between Shimon Peres and Benjamin Netanyahu is often considered the moment Netanyahu won the election.
This meant that in 1999, when there was meant to be another debate between Likud and Labor's candidate Ehud Barak, Barak declined, believing it would help Netanyahu win the election. Barak defeated Netanyahu 56% to 44% in one of Israel's few direct elections for prime minister.
While no further direct head-to-head debates ocurred after 1999, many candidates have challenged sitting prime ministers. The lack of head-to-head debates since 1999 may be attributed to the dissolution of the two-party system in Israel.
Whereas during the main era of debates, two main parties dominated politics, today, many parties compete for the premiership, which makes direct debates less attractive as a format.

BELGRADE, October 4. /TASS/. Bosnia-Herzegovina’s Central Election Commission has announced preliminary results of Sunday’s general elections after counting 90% of votes.
Thus, Denis Becirovic of Bosnia-Hezegovina’s Social Democratic Party is leading in the election of the Bosniak (Slavs professing Islam) member of the BiH Presidency (Presidium) with 38.12%. His rival, Bakir Izetbegovic, the leader of the Party of Democratic Action, is garnering 33.98% of votes.
Darjana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina is number one in the race for the Croatian member of the Presidency with 46.56%. Her rival, Slaven Kovacevic, is scoring 30.54%.
Zeljka Cvijanovic of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats in Republika Srpska is the leader in the election of the Republika Srpska’s member of the Presidency with 55.34%. Her rival, Marinko Bozovic of the opposition, is winning 26.55%.
Republika Srpska’s Prime Minister Savo Minic is winning the elections of the entity’s president with 52.13% of votes. The opposition candidate, Branko Blanusa, currently has 41.95%.
The parties that are receiving the highest number of votes in the elections to the House of Representatives (the lower house of the BiH parliament) are the Party of Democratic Action (19.89%), the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (16.44%), the Social Democratic Party of BiH (9.39%), the Croatian Democratic Union of BiH (8%), and the Safe Srpska movement led by Banja Luka’s mayor, Drasko Stanivukovic (5.99%).
The Alliance of Independent Social Democrats is leading in all constituencies in the elections to the National Assembly (parliament) of Republika Srpska with more than 35%. Its leader Milorad Dodik said earlier that his party and its coalition partners would receive "two thirds of seats."
Under the constitution envisaged by the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina (Dayton Agreement) of 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina is comprised of two entities, namely the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (around 51% of the territory) and the Republic of Srpska (around 49%), as well as the Brcko District. The three key ethno-religious groups, i.e. Bosniaks (Slavs professing Islam), Serbs (Orthodox Christians), and Croats (Catholics), are proportionally represented in the state governance system.

Now, Supreme Court has indicated that in such cases, the parents of the runaway partner have to face the consequences.Hearing such a case, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan revived a 'Look Out Circular' - monitor, trace, or restrict travel of individuals - against the parents of a man who clandestinely took away his three-and-a-half-year-old daughter to the US, without informing his wife, and has refused to bring her back to India."The minor child, at the relevant point of time, aged three-and-a-half years, was taken away by the father to US. The mother is relentlessly trying to get her daughter back. The mother is in a pathetic condition. We have no idea in what circumstances the minor daughter is residing in US with her father, that too a working father," the bench said.It added that all attempts are being made by the man's parents to surreptitiously leave this country and obstruct the course of justice.
"We have stayed the operation of the order passed by Madras High Court setting aside the Look Out Circular," the bench said.It granted the man a last chance to come back to India with the minor child. "We have made ourselves more than clear that he has to come to India within four weeks from the US with her, failing which his parents will have to face severe legal consequences. We have made the parents understand in vernacular," Supreme Court said.
The bench said that if he was not inclined to come to India within four weeks, then he should make necessary arrangements to put the child on board along with an escort. It also asked him to hand over the child to the mother if she reached US."We have passed this order keeping in mind the interest of the child, who was taken-away by her father deceitfully when she was just three-and-a-half years of age. Why should she be deprived of the love, care and affection of her own mother? Why should he stay back in US along with the daughter?" the court said in its order and posted the hearing after a month.

Bosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:42:08 UTC
05:42:08 KST

Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war.
Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that has sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia.
Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war.
With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik’s ally Željka Cvijanović of the rightwing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of the votes to take one of the three seats in the country’s tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by about 30 percentage points.
Speaking at a news conference late on Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska’s assembly, and credited US president Donald Trump’s “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian president Vladimir Putin’s support for the election win.
“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. “We will not give up, but continue for our people … I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.”
About 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.
With more than 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipović of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while the incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency, Denis Bećirović of the Social Democratic party, led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegović, by fewer than three percentage points.
Both Filipović and Bećirović declared victory in their races late on Sunday before all votes were counted.
Bosnia’s central election commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by about 8% from Bosnia’s last election in 2022.
Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.
Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia’s national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country.
At his party’s final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead”.
“It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian ambassador Igor Khalabukov.
Such political and ethnic divisions – in which the country’s Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines – have blocked Bosnia’s progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to work together for reform.
Dragan Bursać, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere.”
“It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursać said.
One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades on from the war, which started in 1992 after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.
Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladić, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.

In total, 15 documents worth 8.5 billion euros were signed following the forum, Shmyhal reported.
He emphasized that Germany is one of Ukraine’s most important and reliable partners.
“We have strong cooperation in the energy and economic sectors. German support has helped us restore damaged infrastructure and strengthen the resilience of our power grid,” Shmyhal noted.

In particular, Shmyhal noted, the possibility of using 12 Siemens Energy gas turbine units for distributed generation is being explored.

Naftogaz and Siemens Energy will collaborate to enhance the resilience and restore Ukraine’s energy system in three areas:
- energy security and infrastructure protection: facility protection, security audits, crisis management, cybersecurity, and rapid recovery;
- modernization of underground gas storage facilities. A project is being developed to supply five gas turbine compressor units to expand our capacity;
- technical cooperation on electricity generation. The possibility of implementing generation based on Siemens Energy solutions and automated control systems is being explored.
Shmyhal thanked German businesses for their active stance and willingness to deepen the partnership to modernize Ukraine’s energy sector and strengthen joint energy security.
As reported by Ukrinform, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday, October 4, on an unannounced visit.
During a joint press conference with Merz in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Germany had allocated a new comprehensive support package for Ukraine totaling 1.3 billion euros.
First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal, during a meeting in Kyiv with German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Katherina Reiche, discussed joint energy support projects for Ukraine, as well as issues related to the supply of liquefied natural gas and the restoration of the shelter at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.

Israel has reacted with anger after the United Kingdom’s Green Party voted to define Zionism as a form of racism.
Israel, as well as British Jewish groups, lashed out on Sunday following the vote by the small political party. The Israeli government declared that it now views the left-leaning Greens as giving “legitimacy to terrorism”.
The Green Party, which received 6 percent of the vote in the UK’s national elections in 2024, said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel.
In a swift response, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the policy went “far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate” and called on other British political parties to condemn the resolution.
“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the ministry wrote on social media.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog labelled the move “a disgrace and a shame”. Writing on social media, he said: “Those who claim the antisemitic lie that ‘Zionism is racism’ deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere.”
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said it is “not Zionism that’s racism, it is the Green Party”.
The Movement for Progressive Judaism, a British group, said: “The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party”.
It added that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others.
During the vote, the Green Party also reaffirmed its “commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel”.
It also reiterated support for “the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”, the party said in a statement.
The motion was backed by a majority of 1,022 to 813. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is running for Parliament in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s London constituency, did not vote.
In an interview with UK media outlet Sky News, the Greens’ co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said that the heavy casualty toll during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and its ongoing attacks were the context for the vote.
The Green Party has five sitting members in the UK’s 650-seat parliament.
Following the passage of the resolution, Polanski and other Green Party members said in a joint statement they would “continue to stand in opposition to genocide, ethnic cleansing, apartheid and the illegal occupation” and “call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government”.

====================================================================================================

Trump Is Promising Health Care Checks Before the Midterms. How Far Will They Go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:38:29 UTC
05:38:29 KST

President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 2 that 20.8 million eligible Medicare enrollees will receive a one-time $90 premium rebate from the government.
It represents the latest payout that the President has made or promised Americans ahead of midterm elections, at a time when 66% of rural voters are worried about affording health care for themselves or their families, according to a KFF/AP poll released Sept. 23. The same survey found that 54% disapproved of Trump’s handling of health care.
The $90 payout is intended to help older Americans pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which jumped by a record amount from 2025 to 2026.
“I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending ‘Checks’ of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts,” the President wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump said the payments would come from the roughly $2 billion Medicare Improvement Fund, which Congress established in 2008 to improve Original Medicare, the traditional program covering hospital and medical services. The fund’s authorized uses include adjusting payments to health care providers, but its mandate is broader than those payments alone.
The Administration is presenting the rebates as another way to improve the program by making coverage more affordable. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said in an FAQ that the payments would put money “in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries.” It does not spell out the legal basis for using the fund to send checks directly to enrollees.
The CMS said most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 payment by direct deposit in early October, while others will receive a mailed check.
The Medicare rebates follow Trump’s Sept. 10 announcement of $500 refunds for some Affordable Care Act enrollees, who the Administration claims paid excessive fees under Biden.
Trump touted these refunds during a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, during which he claimed that his Administration had already sent out nearly a million $500 refund checks—with about 70,000 going to families in Ohio.
“You'll be getting them in the next couple of days,” he told the Ohio crowd. He also said, without evidence, that Democrats “kept millions and millions of dollars” from Americans.
The White House said that the refunds come from a surplus of ACA marketplace user fees collected under the Biden Administration, which it claimed exceeded the amount needed to operate the federal exchange.
For eligible ACA enrollees, the $500 refund could help cover health expenses, but it is a one-time payment—not a reduction in their ongoing insurance premiums.
The distinction between a one-time payment and recurring costs is crucial, says Lindsay Allen, a health economist and policy researcher at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine.
“Getting $90 once doesn't change anyone's Medicare costs,” Allen says.
According to the CMS, the standard monthly Medicare Part B premium rose from $185 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026. That amounts to an additional $214.80 over a full year, meaning a $90 rebate would cover about 42% of the annual increase for eligible enrollees paying the standard premium—or less than half of a single month’s payment.
Why are older Americans feeling financial pressure?
According to the American Association of Retired Persons’ Financial Security Trends Survey, this year saw a growing number of Americans ages 50 and older feeling financially squeezed.
New census data this year also found that the poverty rate has increased the most for Americans 65 and older, growing from 9.1% in 2020 to 13.1% in 2025.
Those pressures also underpin expectations for next year’s cost-of-living adjustment from the Social Security Administration.
The Senior Citizens League projects a 3.5% increase for 2027, though the official adjustment will be announced Oct. 14. An increase of that size would raise average monthly benefits from $1,941.76 to $2,009.72. These annual adjustments are designed to help ensure that beneficiaries’ monthly payments help them keep pace with inflation, and an increase—potentially the largest cost-of-living adjustment since 2023—underscores the continuing pressure of rising prices on older Americans.
Some analysts note the timing of the payouts, with the midterms approaching and Republicans facing a potential backlash over Trump’s second term. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report says the party is on track to lose its House majority.
Public dissatisfaction extends across the economy and the war in Iran. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 1 found that 65% of Americans attributed higher-than-usual prices to Trump’s policies, while 64% said he had gone too far in imposing tariffs. The same survey found that 69% believed the Iran war had not been worth fighting. About half (49%) of respondents said they were “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July.
The payments also come as changes to federal health policy threaten to add to some beneficiaries’ costs, raising questions about how much lasting relief the rebates can provide.
How much will Trump’s Medicare rebate help?
Several Trump Administration policy decisions will soon begin affecting Medicare and other health care programs for senior adults.
The Administration announced in July that it would end the Medicare Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration program on Jan. 1, 2027—a year earlier than originally planned, which is something that advocate groups like Medicare Rights Center worry “will unnecessarily erode beneficiary choice, health, and financial security.”
“It is likely to make it harder for older adults and people with disabilities to access and afford needed care,” the group said in its response to the decision in July, urging the Administration to reconsider.
Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill was also signed into law in summer 2025 and had massive implications for older adults’ health care benefits—including delaying the implementation of a 2023 rule that would have streamlined enrolling in the Medicare Savings Programs, which help low-income beneficiaries pay for Medicare premiums and cost-sharing, until 2034.
Allen doubts that the refunds can offset the big issue at hand: “Medicare costs are increasing every year, but incomes for older adults aren’t.”
William Dow, a professor of health policy at University of California, Berkeley, reiterates Allen’s point, saying that the check “will have minimal effects in mitigating the overall increased cost of living among older adults.”
“This is particularly true because lower-income Medicare enrollees, for whom every dollar is most important, are not eligible for the checks,” Dow says. Beneficiaries whose premiums are already paid by Medicaid do not qualify, according to the White House.
“This makes sense given that the payment is a premium rebate and these beneficiaries don’t pay their own premiums. It does, however, mean that the payment leaves out the most financially vulnerable people in the program,” Allen says.
She points out that premiums are likely to go up again in 2027.
“People will get a small one-time check before the election, and then likely hear about next year's premium increase after it,” she says, calling it “notable” that people are likely to receive these checks within the next few weeks, just shortly before the midterm elections.
She believes that short-term relief might sway some voters—even though those people will continue to feel the premium increases “every month” after. According to health policy nonprofit KFF, the standard Part B premium has doubled in costs over the last decade and it is projected to increase even further in 2027.
“The payment is also limited relative to everyday expenses,” Allen says. “At current prices, $90 will get you about one tank of gas.”
Dow says that the move might eventually backfire, arguing that distributing roughly $1.9 billion in rebates will leave less money available for future improvements to Medicare.
“While perhaps good politics on the eve of an election, these checks are being paid from a fund intended by Congress to improve Medicare operations,” he says. “By diverting these funds, the long-term net effect will instead be to undermine Medicare operations.”

Suspected ShinyHunters hacker detained in Jordan, cooperating with FBI, sources say
A suspected member of ShinyHunters, the hacking group that claimed responsibility last month for defacing the FBI's website, was detained in Jordan this week and is cooperating with the investigators, according to U.S. officials.
Jordanian authorities detained Saif al-Din Khader this week, according to two U.S. officials and another source with knowledge of the matter.
ShinyHunters, a notorious cybercrime group, has claimed responsibility for a series of high-profile data breaches and has asserted, without public verification, that it obtained data on every FBI employee. It is unclear how many other alleged hackers may be involved, a U.S. source told CBS News.
The FBI declined to comment on the arrest but said in a statement that "the Bureau continues to aggressively investigate the recent Cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters, having already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects and we will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice."
The arrest was first reported by Reuters.
Last month, ShinyHunters claimed in communications posted on the dark web and exchanges with multiple media outlets that it stole 2 to 3 terabytes of data related to FBI workers. The hackers claimed to have used a new vulnerability with Oracle PeopleSoft, a human resources management program.
A second suspected member of the group, identified as a 24-year-old from Amsterdam, was arrested on Sept. 15 on suspicion of being a member of ShinyHunters, Dutch National Police and the FBI previously reported. That means he was already in custody days before ShinyHunters announced it had hacked the FBI jobs website, which was first reported on Sept. 22 by 404 Media.
Dutch police did not identify the suspect by name, but sources familiar with the case confirmed to CBS News that the man is Pepijn van der Stap.
In a statement to Reuters, ShinyHunters said Van der Stap had "no association" with the group and that Dutch police were incompetent.

Israel wear black armbands in Nations League draw against Ireland to mark Hamas attack
JERUSALEM - Israel’s players wore black armbands in their Nations League draw against Ireland on Oct 4 to commemorate the victims of Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023 attack, after Irish players wore them to protest the war in Gaza.
The simple black armbands were inscribed with the numbers “7.10” to mark the date of the attack.
Just as in last week’s first match in Hungary which Ireland won 3-0, the Irish players again bowed their heads during the Israeli anthem and the teams refused to shake hands before the 1-1 draw, this time played in the small Serbian town of Backa Topola.
The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had refused to host Israel on Irish soil for security reasons, following boycott calls.
On Oct 4, Troy Parrott put Ireland ahead from the penalty spot after 39 minutes after Dor Peretz fouled Jimmy Dunne.
The Real Betis striker has now scored 10 of the last 13 competitive goals for the Republic.
But Peretz stabbed in an equaliser two minutes after half-time, sending in from close range after a shot deflected off Ireland defender Liam Scales and into his path.
The result complicates Ireland’s qualification task as they now lie third in Group 3 of League B behind Austria and Kosovo. Israel are bottom with two points.
The Israeli Football Association said on Oct 4 that the request to wear black armbands had been approved by European football’s governing body UEFA.
The Hamas-led attack was the deadliest in Israeli history and killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.
The massive Israeli offensive in response has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
The two matches against Israel have sparked controversy in Ireland, which has long supported the Palestinian cause.
Ireland’s 2-2 draw against Austria in Dublin on Oct 1 was twice briefly interrupted by demonstrations in support of the Palestinians.
Israel has been unable to host international matches on its own soil because of security risks since the outbreak of the war in Gaza.
The first match went ahead in Hungary instead, with Ireland beating Israel following a turbulent build-up in which the Irish squad voted to fulfil the fixture after goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu pulled out a day before the game.
On Oct 3, Ireland’s press conference in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists, including one about an Omani pilot’s attack on a flydubai flight headed for Tel Aviv earlier in the week.
The Icelander sparked a diplomatic row over the games in September by saying: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”
The Israeli association accused him of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy”. 
On Oct 4, Hallgrimsson said in hindsight he would have done things differently.
“Today, I would think I did a mistake there because my feelings and my opinion should be set aside when I’m spokesman for an organisation and a group,” he said in Serbia. AFP

Labuschagne set for Test after first ton in 11 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:28:59 UTC
05:28:59 KST

Marnus Labuschagne has found form with the bat, with a century days out from the first Test against South Africa.
Labuschagne retired after making 111 off 89 balls in a drawn game against an Invitation XI in Potchefstroom.
What's next?
Australia plays the first of three Tests against South Africa in Durban starting on Friday.
Marnus Labuschagne has responded to the debate over whether he merits a place in Australia's Test future by just doing what he likes doing best — scoring runs.
After a difficult year, the under-pressure 32-year-old chose the most timely moment to score his first century in any form of cricket for 11 months in Potchefstroom, just five days before Australia play their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.
Former skipper Ricky Ponting had joined the chorus that Labuschagne's place in Australia had become "untenable" after three years and 43 Tests without a Test ton, capped by three failures in the recent Bangladesh series.
Yet the South African-born batter looks sure to fill the number three spot once more in the first Test that starts in Durban on Friday after his swift century against a modest Cricket South Africa Invitation XI attack.
Labuschagne was largely untroubled as he raced to a 76-ball ton, going on to 111 from 89, decorated with 19 fours, before retiring to let his colleagues also get in some batting practice on the final day of the two-day warm-up match.
They enjoyed the opportunity too, with Steve Smith also retiring after making 61 while Alex Carey, fresh from his fine form in the third ODI, hit another half-century (57) as Pat Cummins' Australian side rattled up 6-368 in the drawn game.
Smith, who received a 12-month ban when captain for his role in altering the condition of the ball with sandpaper at Cape Town on the infamous tour eight years ago, is back with a group of other survivors from that tour — Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw.
Those four could all play on Friday.
Renshaw looked completely recovered from a knock to his right wrist, but may feel he missed out by being dismissed for 32 off his 50 balls, as may his fellow opener Travis Head (21 off 22 balls).
Beau Webster brushed off a few cobwebs with his 42 off 88 balls before he retired.
All eyes, though, were on Labuschagne, who even had a bit of local support as he took the crease at Senwes Park, a venue less than 50km from where he was born in Klerksdorp and the emotional scene of his first ODI hundred for Australia back in 2020.
Australia will see it as a useful workout after they gave 11 bowlers a run-out on Saturday when the Invitation XI declared on 7-318 after a century from former Proteas captain Neil Brand.
Meanwhile, South Africa paceman Anrich Nortje is in line for a remarkable return to first-class cricket after an absence of three-and-a-half years to help the injury-hit Proteas' attack.
With fitness doubts over key strike bowler Kagiso Rabada and three others, Nortje could return to Tests for the first time since March 2023 after a series of back and hip problems that left him concentrating on white-ball formats to reduce the strain on his body.
"I'll be very excited if I can put my Test cap on again. Growing up, it's the format you want to play," he said on Sunday, the day before he's expected to be named in South Africa's Test squad of 15.

The Coalition dropped its policy of reaching net zero emissions by 2050 under former Liberal leader Sussan Ley.

The shadow minister tells ABC Radio National Breakfast Australia has "serious" domestic challenges that need to be addressed.
"I do think that we're much better off if we're helping the Pacific with a strong economy where we are making sure that we're looking after Australians," Tehan says.

Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen hasn't been able to outline the final cost of organising the pre-COP meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu.

Assistant minister highlights figures showing rise in legal tobacco sales
Assistant Minister Julian Hill has seized on figures showing legal tobacco sales rose 55 per cent in Queensland following stronger enforcement.
The state's sales rose 55 per cent in the first month after new enforcement laws took effect in November and remained 40 to 45 per cent above previous levels for the following six months.
Federal Labor has been under pressure to reduce the tobacco excise after the Coalition and One Nation pledged to drastically reduce the tax.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Hill says strong licensing laws, tougher penalties, long-term closure orders and landlord penalties are effective in tackling illicit tobacco.

"Imagine a world where you wiped out all tobacco excise, the illegal cigarettes are still cheaper. You still have to go after the crooks and shut the shop and disrupt the criminal syndicates."

"If you go to build something that's first of type, you're going to pay a lot more money than if you build something that's more affordable."
But Labor MP Josh Burns has called the plan "mad" and has accused Joyce of wearing a "tinfoil hat".

Brazilians head to polls in pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:12:22 UTC
05:12:22 KST

Polls close in Brazil’s pivotal election
Polls have closed in Brazil’s hotly contested presidential election, which could reshape the country’s domestic and foreign policy.
The race is dominated by incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Lula is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term in office. More than a dozen other candidates are also on the ballot.
Polls released on the eve of the election showed Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck. Quaest put them at 46% and 45%, respectively, while Datafolha had Lula at 45% and Bolsonaro at 42%, with both surveys showing a statistical tie. If neither candidate wins more than half of votes, a runoff will be held on October 25. All other candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their endorsements could prove important in a second round.
Brazilians will also elect all 513 federal congress members, 54 of the country’s 81 senators, 27 governors and some regional legislatures.
Lula campaigned on his left-leaning Workers’ Party platform, promising continued welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. He has framed the vote as a choice between “strengthening democracy and barbarism.”
Bolsonaro called for “change,” blaming Lula’s policies for high living costs and promising tougher security policies and tax cuts. The 45-year-old senator for Rio de Janeiro has also leaned heavily on the image of his father, known to supporters as “mito” – “the legend.”
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced to 27 years behind bars over attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 presidential election, which he lost to Lula. He has denied wrongdoing. He spent several months in prison after breaking house arrest monitoring rules before being hospitalized in March 2026 over health issues and eventually transferred back to “temporary” house arrest that has since been extended.
Why does this vote matter?
Brazil is a founding member of BRICS and has played a prominent role in the group. Under Lula, Brasilia has pursued a policy focused on strengthening multipolarity and resisting Western pressure, particularly from Washington.
The Trump administration has placed renewed emphasis on US dominance in the Western Hemisphere under what it calls the “Donroe Doctrine,” a modern reinterpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine.
Washington has said it intends to strengthen US influence across the Americas while preventing rival powers, particularly China, from gaining strategic footholds there.
Opposing ‘colonization’
During his current term, Lula has repeatedly criticized the US over what he described as attempts to undermine multipolarity and impose its will on other nations.
Last year, India and Brazil stepped up talks on trade and investment after both countries were hit with 50% tariffs by the US. Lula also called for a coordinated BRICS response to Washington’s tariff policies, accusing Trump of attempts to “dismantle multilateralism” and promote “unilateralism, where he negotiates one-on-one with other countries.”
The Brazilian president also sharply condemned the US kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in early 2026. In March, he proposed boosting defense cooperation with South Africa to reduce reliance on foreign weapons, arguing that both nations could be vulnerable to “invasion.”
In late September, he openly accused Trump of seeking to “colonize” Brazil and gain control of its natural resources. “What Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, to take our wealth, steal our future and leave us behind,” he stated at the time.
‘Trump’s candidate’?
Flavio Bolsonaro, whom Lula has described as “Trump’s candidate,” has emphasized his affinity with the US president and repeatedly praised him, while denying receiving assistance from Washington for his campaign. He has insisted that Brazil should seek better deals with the US, including on rare earth minerals – a topic that has been repeatedly invoked by US President Donald Trump in his talks with various nations, including Ukraine and Russia.
The senator also promised a “flood of investments” from the US if he wins. “Brazil and the United States will once again have a high-level and long-term relationship, including the largest trade and investment agreement in our history!” Bolsonaro wrote in a post on X in June.
He has also vowed to “truly combat Brazilian terrorist organizations and restore sovereignty to more than 50 million Brazilians who live in areas dominated by them,” without specifying which groups he meant.
Bolsonaro has also reportedly pledged to join the US campaign against drug cartels. The American military has at times targeted boats supposedly belonging to traffickers, killing dozens of people.
Shadow of interference
Brazilian authorities have opened a probe into allegations that the US government funded activities aimed at interfering in the election and undermining the legitimacy of the country’s Supreme Federal Court, Agencia Brasil reported on Friday.
That followed a report by the Guardian earlier in the week, claiming that the White House had planned to allocate $1 million for a project titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.”
US social media giant Meta also blocked the advertising account on Facebook used by Lula’s campaign, preventing it from running new ads just days before the first round. The account was restored later the same day, with Meta providing no immediate explanation.
In September, Lula cited a confidential assessment by the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, which warned that a risk of US interference in the vote was allegedly at a “critical level.”
Trump avoided openly endorsing any candidates ahead of the elections but stated he was following the vote “very closely.”
“Brazil is a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. These are very important elections,” he said on Thursday.
Moscow has expressed its hope that the Sunday vote would be held “without any adverse external interference.” “We are open to… continuing our cooperation with our Brazilian partners across the entire agenda,” the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Latin American Department, Aleksandr Shetinin, told TASS.

Metric trusts to resume trading
The three listed private credit funds operated by the $40 billion Metric Credit Partners that were suspended on the ASX last week following valuation discrepancies identified by their auditor will resume trading this morning.
As we reported last week, the Metrics Income Opportunities Trust, Metrics Master Income Trust and Metrics Real Estate Multi-Strategy Fund were suspended after auditors KPMG "found certain amounts and information in the audited 2026 financial report will differ from those in the Preliminary report" of all three trusts.

CSL signs deal to develop kidney and liver treatment
Australia's biotech heavyweight CSL has signed a major deal with a Swiss-based drug firm Alentis to co-develop and promote a treatment for a rare autoimmune kidney and liver disease.
The collaboration centres on the drug Lixudebartm, which is currently being evaluated in an ongoing phase two trial on patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).
AAV is a rare autoimmune disease that causes inflammation and damage in small and medium blood vessels, potentially affecting multiple organs such as kidneys and liver.
The associated RPGN is characterised by a rapid loss of kidney function in a matter of days.
"We believe Lixudebart has the potential to become an important new therapeutic option to help improve kidney function and prevent progression to end-stage kidney disease," CSL head of R&D Bill Mezzanotte said.
CSL will make an initial payment to Alentis of $US355 million, with Alentis eligible to receive up to an additional $US1.2 billion in commercial milestone payments.
If commercialised, global profits will be shared 55% to CSL and 45% to Alentis.
"Our collaboration with Alentis reflects CSL's commitment to building a leading global nephrology franchise and our strategic intent to create high-value external partnerships," Dr Mezzanotte said.

Is the bond market rout overdone?
Capital Economics markets strategy team posted an interesting note asking the question "was the bond market rout" — that is, falling bond prices and rising interest rates — "overdone?"
"Perhaps" seems to be the answer, but that doesn't mean equity markets are about to be given a leg up if interest rates stop rising and edge lower.
Quite the opposite, according to Capital Economics (CE), which sees see the AI-driven equity rally as bubble waiting to burst.
CE noted that markets in the past quarter have been dominated by three stories that have been important all year: the waxing and waning of investors' enthusiasm for AI-exposed equities, big swings in commodity prices, and a sharp rise in bond yields.
"We think all three trends are approaching turning points," CE's Chief Markets Economist Jonas Goltermann wrote in a note.
"We suspect the AI-driven equity rally has become stretched and will turn into a rout at some point.
"We also expect commodity prices to fall back, with the caveat that energy prices will continue to depend heavily on developments in the Strait of Hormuz.
"And we think that government bonds will recover as tightening cycles underwhelm expectations."
On the bond rout, Mr Goltermann expects a reversal before too long.
"We expect the sell-off in DM (Developed Market) government bonds to unwind over the coming year or so as energy prices drop back and most central banks tighten policy by less than is now discounted, generating good returns from bonds.
"We think corporate bond spreads will widen markedly given our view that the AI stock market boom will turn to bust, especially given that huge AI-related bond issuance has increased the direct exposure of that asset class to AI."
CE's view is that the AI boom's day of reckoning may be sooner rather than later.
"While timing such crashes is hard, our forecasts envisage one happening next year. That allows for the possibility of a final 'blow-off' phase in which tech stocks, in particular, make further gains before heading sharply lower."
Key Event
OPEC+ agrees to keep November oil output targets steady
OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday.
The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the US-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.
"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to US President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $US100 a barrel, up from about $US73 before the Iran war started in late February.
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.

The hack of Medicare by an OpenAI agent, which followed other hacks by AI agents, illuminated the fact that these companies are not building a screwdriver that exists only as a tool for humans; they're building agents that turn passive AI into active autonomy.

Protests by school students in France are continuing; on Monday, up to 500 schools will not hold classes
Kyiv • UNN
Up to 500 schools in France will be closed on Monday due to student protests. Students and education unions are preparing a new action for Tuesday.
Massive protests by high school students are continuing in France. They began back in September and have spread to many cities across the country. On Monday, classes will be suspended at between 400 and 500 schools, while on Tuesday students and education unions are preparing a new nationwide action, Le Monde reports, writes UNN.
Details
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray said that approximately the same number of institutions had also not been operating on Friday. According to him, schools are being closed where it is impossible to guarantee safety, logistical problems have arisen, or staff have become direct targets of attacks.
The most difficult situation is expected in the Île-de-France region, where more than 160 schools will not operate on Monday—more than a third of the region's total.
The protests will continue
The movement began on September 17 in Île-de-France and later spread to other cities across the country. Students are demanding increased education funding, the filling of vacant teaching positions, repairs to dilapidated school buildings, changes to excessively packed schedules, and improvements to the university admissions system, Parcoursup.
According to the minister, 78 education-sector employees have been affected since the protests began, while 24 schools have been set on fire or damaged by vandals. In Île-de-France, the damage is already estimated at €7 million.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu instructed authorities to resume classes wherever the security situation permits, and to speed up the replacement of absent teachers and the filling of vacancies.
However, after talks with the government, protesters said they had not received sufficiently concrete solutions. For Tuesday, October 6, student organizations announced the "third act" of the protests, which education unions also plan to join with a strike.

SIR strikes at heart of Constitution: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan

2026-10-04
20:04:02 UTC
