He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Myanmar migrants make return to war-torn nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:38 UTC
01:38:38 KST

Nearly 1,500 Burmese migrants from Malaysia returned to their war-ravaged home country yesterday under an opaque repatriation scheme that rights monitors say cannot assure their safety.
Dozens of migrants were transported on buses to a Buddhist monastery hall for immigration and health checks, after the returnees arrived by Myanmar Navy ships that docked at the nearby base in Thanlyin.
“I haven’t met my family yet,” said Kyaw Swar Thein, 53, who worked in a coffee shop in Malaysia before he was arrested there. He said he suffered scabies while in detention for a year and eight months — one reason he wanted to come home. Now his future seems unclear.
Photo: EPA
“I do not hope for anything,” he said among the rows of men sat cross-legged on the floor, some wearing T-shirts reading “We love Myanmar.”
The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.
Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centers, but the UN and rights groups have raised concerns that Myanmar migrants had little choice.
Hundreds of families with vehicles gathered at dawn to collect their relatives outside the naval base, some holding up paper signs with photographs or the names of their loved ones.
A naval official dashed hopes of immediate reunions for most.
“You cannot take them right away,” he shouted into a megaphone, saying returnees would first be brought to different locations in the Yangon region.
One woman said she was looking for her 19-year-old brother who was arrested in Malaysia soon after he arrived there three months ago.
“We saw his name on the list of returnees but we couldn’t go inside to find him,” said the woman, who declined to give her name for security reasons.
Three Myanmar Navy ships carrying migrants docked at the Thanlyin base early yesterday, a naval official, whom AFP has kept anonymous as he was not authorized to speak to media, said
The ships left Malaysia on Tuesday carrying 1,476 migrants, mostly men, the Myanmar government said — the first of 5,000 that Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says Myanmar agreed to take back.
“Our main concern is his arrival won’t be safe,” said the sister of one migrant who had told his family he expected to be sent aboard the ships.
There are also concerns members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group after Anwar announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya.
Members of the ethnic group fled Myanmar en masse following a military crackdown starting in 2017, which rights experts say amounted to genocide.
Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but Kuala Lumpur has not responded to an AFP query about the number onboard.
Myanmar says the returnees completed sentences for immigration offences in Malaysia.
Monitor organizations such as Fortify Rights report dire conditions in the detention centers.
The UN refugee agency said this past week its staff were not allowed to meet migrants to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed.”
Malaysia is already moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens.
Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme.
Myanmar pledged last month that returns would be “safe and dignified.”
However, Fortify Rights senior human rights specialist Yap Lay Sheng said: “There’s no telling how the regime would treat returnees.”
Myanmar’s civil war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, monitor ACLED said — including 50 in a military airstrike late last month.
“This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses,” UN rights chief Volker Turk said on Tuesday.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:33 UTC
01:38:33 KST

1. 不該把一個生病的孩子獨自留在家裡。
ˇ It’s not advisable to leave a sick child all alone at home.
χ It’s not advisable to leave an ill child all alone at home.
Photo: AdobeStock l 照片:AdobeStock
註︰ill 和 sick 都可用作補語形容詞，例如：
〔英語〕I have been ill/unwell for two weeks.
〔美語〕I have been sick for two weeks.
但作為修飾形容詞置於名詞之前時，英美都用 sick，不用 ill，如 a sick man /woman, a sick child 等。
2. 昨天整天都在下大雨。
ˇ Heavy rain fell all day long yesterday.
ˇ There was heavy rain all day long yesterday.
χ A great rain fell all day long yesterday.
註︰中文裡的「大」，不一定對應英語中的 big 或 great，試對照下列中英文：
大風：a strong / heavy wind、大雪：a heavy snow
3. 許多夜晚他餓著肚子去睡覺。
ˇ Many nights, he went to bed with an empty stomach.
χ Many nights, he went to bed with a hungry stomach.
註︰中文「餓著肚子」，在英語中是「空著肚子」，應用 an empty stomach。
4. 學好鋼琴不容易。
ˇ It is not easy to master the piano.
ˇ It is difficult/hard to master the piano.
χ It is uneasy to master the piano.
註︰easy 作「容易」解時，它的反義詞是 hard 或 difficult；easy 作「安心」、「舒適」等解時，它的反義詞是 uneasy。例如：
It is an easy chair.
He leads an easy life.
He feels uneasy about the result of the examination.
（他擔心自己的考試成績。）
5. 這個座位有人坐嗎？
ˇ Is this seat taken/available?
χ Is this seat empty?
註︰empty 是 full 的反義詞，如 an empty box, an empty bottle, an empty pot, an empty cup。available 指「未被佔用/可以使用」之意。試比較下列句子：
available 指未被佔用//可以使用：
We must find a room available for the meeting.
empty 指空無一物：
The empty room looks especially large.
Exercises
A. 大雨後河水淹沒街道。
The river flooded the streets after a __________ rain.
1. great
2. grave
3. serious
4. heavy
B. 這個座位空著嗎？
Is this seat __________ ?
1. hollow
2. taken
3. empty
4. devoid
Answers: A. 4 B. 2

www.bookman.com.tw

The ‘intangible economy’  is making everyone miserable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:32 UTC
01:38:32 KST

These are the best of times for Americans — at least economically, and at least on paper. They have never been richer or more prosperous as a nation. Living standards and life expectancy are at all-time highs. Yet, it feels like the economy is broken.
What explains this? Consider how few of the things we own are physical anymore. Our economy is increasingly built on intangibles, and it may be hard to feel satisfied when so much of what we have is no longer in the physical realm.
Take wealth. More young people are investing in the stock market instead of housing. It has been a wise choice: The stock market has offered a higher return and less risk for the past decade. Stock investing does not require a down payment or tie the buyer to a single place in their prime skill-building years. Rising stock values are a big reason why Gen Z is the richest generation for their age.
Illustration: Yusha
However, owning stocks is an intangible form of wealth. They own a share of the US economy, but it is hard to look at Amazon.com Inc. and feel as though part of it is theirs. More of the US stock market, too, is made up of companies whose value is their intellectual property, another intangible.
Compare this to owning a home. Someone can physically own property. They can put money or even their own labor into renovating their kitchen. They know their neighbors, feel part of a community and have an interest in investing in both. I do not look at fellow S&P 500 Index owners and feel a common sense of purpose, although theoretically I should.
The sense of community and belonging has been replaced with social lives that are less tangible as well. More socialization takes place in the virtual world. We spend less time with other people in person or even on the phone. We buy more online rather than see people and goods when we shop. This may leave us feeling more disconnected and lonely, even if we have more connections and can communicate with people all over the world.
Our human capital has become more intangible. More of us work in the services sector and build skills oriented to it, rather than making things. Service jobs often earn more and are less physically arduous, but there is no output from our labor. Journalists rarely see their ideas on the printed page anymore. The premium placed on knowledge work has contributed to income and wealth inequality. Wages are lower in a physical economy but less dispersed.
These shifts may help explain the backlash to data centers. Building factories tends to be popular and seen as a political triumph. Data centers could bring economic benefits to a community as they create construction jobs and are associated with growth. Yet, they have only been met with suspicion.
Some of the distrust springs from the belief that they cause pollution and drive up electricity bills. Another point of friction is their newness and the difficulty of understanding what they produce and to whose benefit, particularly when the fear of job loss to artificial intelligence looms large. It is not like making a toaster, even if data centers could be a sign of a much more advanced and wealthy economy.
Before we go full luddite, quit our jobs and live off the land in Alaska, it is important to remember that the intangible economy is why some people are richer and live longer lives. Today’s technological innovations reward knowledge and expertise much more than the tangible world ever valued physical labor. We also do much less physical labor, which is one reason many people live longer and healthier lives.
So why are the benefits harder to feel good about? We are social creatures who evolved to compete for finite resources. This new world is less zero sum, since knowledge is infinite, but it leaves us completing for status and attention instead, which can be less satisfying and more ephemeral than a big house or a chunk of gold. It creates new status games, such as social media, that we cannot ever really win.
We also just enjoy stuff. A large, beautiful house may bring more satisfaction than a one-bedroom rental apartment and a $2 million brokerage account balance.
I am optimistic we are not doomed to a life of misery that is devoid of meaning. It just takes time for norms to change. Growing their own food once felt like the most honest work compared to having a boss and working in a factory. We may still have a romantic attachment to the idea of farming, but few people want to be subsistence farmers.
What we consider valuable and meaningful is always evolving and sometimes the transition takes time because the economy moves faster than our norms and culture do. This process can be destabilizing and isolating. Eventually we find ways to connect and rebuild community in new ways. Perhaps we will get to the point where owning nothing tangible will be enough, if we own a lot on paper.
Allison Schrager is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering economics. A senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, she is author of Worth the Risk: The Seven Myths That Keep Us From Taking the Chances We Need to Take. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

The Los Angeles Dodgers, chasing a rare World Series three-peat, on Saturday opened their MLB playoff campaign with a 5-3 win over Atlanta as the Tampa Bay Rays rode a one-hit gem from pitcher Drew Rasmussen to score a 1-0 win over the New York Yankees.
Six strong innings from pitcher Tarik Skubal, and home runs from Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker and Max Muncy propelled the Dodgers over the Braves.
Skubal, the reigning two-time Cy Young Award-winner acquired from Detroit at the trade deadline in August, delivered in his first post-season start for the Dodgers, settling down after surrendering an opening single to retire 15 straight batters.
Photo: AP
In sizzling, 38°C temperatures at Dodger Stadium, Skubal gave up just two hits, including a solo homer to Sean Murphy in the sixth, and had ample support from the Dodgers offense as Los Angeles seized a 1-0 lead in the best-of-five National League division series.
“I think I was just trying to match the temperature out there,” said Skubal, whose fastball hit 163kph in the second inning. “It was a hot one.”
Hernandez gave the Dodgers a 2-0 lead with a 431-foot fourth inning blast off Atlanta relief pitcher Victor Mederos.
Tucker doubled the lead with a two-run shot in the sixth inning with Muncy adding a solo homer two batters later.
Ozzie Albies belted a two-run homer for the Braves to slice the deficit to 5-3 in the ninth inning before the Dodgers closed it out.
The game was one of four second-round series openers on Saturday.
In Florida, Rasmussen held the Yankees without a hit through eight and two-thirds innings.
Yankees catcher Austin Wells broke up his bid for just the fourth no-hitter in MLB post-season history with a double down the first-base line with two out in the eighth.
However, Wells’ inexplicable attempt to reach third saw him thrown out on a perfect relay from Victor Mesa Jr to shortstop Taylor Walls to third baseman Junior Caminero.
“Just obviously not a good decision there,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “But [the] biggest issue is just Rasmussen shutting us down.”
Rasmussen struck out 10 and walked two over eight innings in front of a raucous 40,000-strong crowd at Tropicana Field to make Jonathan Aranda’s third-inning home run off Gerrit Cole stand up.
The Chicago White Sox, fueled by a two-run home run from Munetaka Murakami, beat the Guardians 3-0 in Cleveland for a 1-0 lead in their American League division series.
After three straight seasons with 100 or more defeats the White Sox finished the regular season with an 84-74 record, snagging the sixth seed in the American League and ousting the Houston Astros in two games in the Wild Card round.
In the late game, National League top seeds the Milwaukee Brewers came from behind to dig out a nail-biting 3-2 victory over the in-form San Diego Padres.
The Padres, who arrived in the playoffs in blistering form, took a 2-0 lead in the top of the second inning after Luis Campusano drove in a run for Xander Bogaerts before Ethan Salas crossed home plate on a fielder’s choice.
However, Jackson Chourio’s two-run home run knotted it at 2-2 in the bottom of the third before William Contreras’s solo shot in the seventh gave the Brewers the lead.
There was controversy in the ninth inning though when Ty France launched what looked destined to be a home run — giving the Padres a 4-3 lead — into the right field.
France’s mammoth blast cannoned off the closed roof of Milwaukee’s home stadium and was caught by Chourio, and the Brewers then got the final out to wrap up victory.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) would intensify “gray zone” activities around Taiwan during his fourth term, further undermining regional stability, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said on Saturday.
Xi is expected to secure a fourth five-year term at the 21st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party next year.
As a free and democratic country, Taiwan has followed a starkly different national development than authoritarian China, Chiu said at the Chungshan Youth Academic Conference hosted by the National Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall and National Sun Yat-sen University.
Photo: AP
Since Xi took power, China has failed to achieve freedom and democracy, instead regressing into an authoritarian system like that which Sun Yat-sen (孫逸仙), a founder of the Republic of China, sought to overthrow, Chiu said.
China has shown three extreme political trends in the past 10 years, including centralizing power and shifting it largely onto one person, promoting fervent nationalism that fuels a provocative foreign policy and framing taking over Taiwan as a historic mission, he said.
China has tightened its authoritarian grip at home, while using nationalism to drive military expansion in the region, pushing the country toward an unprecedented form of “new totalitarianism,” he said.
While China claims that different forms of government are not an obstacle to unification, these differences are the root of cross-strait divisions, Chiu said.
Taiwanese chose a free and democratic way of life that they are not willing to give up, he said.
During his fourth term, Xi would step up “gray zone” activity aimed at expanding China’s jurisdiction in the region, following an approach of “governing before unification,” he said.
Xi would also seek international recognition of his territorial claims and push more actively for a “one country, two systems” framework with Taiwan, he added.
China plans to hold events marking Sun’s 160th birthday this year, as it continues to distort Sun’s views to promote unification and integration with Taiwan, Chiu said.
People engaging in cross-strait exchanges should follow regulations and be aware of mainstream sentiment, he said, urging them not to echo China’s interpretation of history and become tools for Beijing’s “united front” efforts.

Groups blast police raid on gay bar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:26 UTC
01:38:26 KST

Civic groups yesterday protested what they called the police’s excessively forceful raid on a Taipei gay bar on Saturday, calling on police to apologize, protect marginalized groups and stop stigmatizing LGBTQ culture.
Police from Taipei’s Wanhua Precinct on Saturday afternoon raided the bar Commander D under a warrant following alleged reports of nudity and indecent behavior.
At the protest held near Ximending’s (西門町) Red House yesterday, the civic groups referred to witnesses who called the raid “heavy-handed,” saying that officers refused to show a warrant, ordered people not to talk or use their phones, behaved arrogantly, insulted LGBTQ people and detained dozens of people in for questioning.
Photo: Reuters
Police made discriminatory remarks about people with disabilities and handcuffed the bar manager, forcing him to kneel, they quoted witnesses as saying, adding a reporter accompanied police into the bar and took photos, ignoring principles about keeping information pertaining to an investigation private.
It is unacceptable for something like this to happen in 2026 in Taiwan, especially considering that Taiwan proclaims itself East Asia’s most progressive country, they added.
The operation lasted five hours, but police reportedly told people at the scene they were only checking people’s identities.
The Wanhua police should explain the operation and apologize for the officers’ conduct and discriminatory remarks, the groups said, adding that the Taipei City Police Department needs to explain their discriminatory law enforcement and hold those responsible accountable.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) must explain the instances of discriminatory enforcement this year and evaluate whether Taipei is truly LGBTQ-friendly, they said.
Kang Yang, a protester, said he was angry the raid had happened, particularly during Pride Month.
“I’m not cool with this,” he said. “This city used to claim that it was queer-friendly.”
In addition to protesting, the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association and nine other LGBTQ groups issued a joint statement yesterday condemning the raid as a repeat of LGBTQ oppression seen 30 years ago.
It is unacceptable for the Taipei City Government to promote itself internationally as LGBTQ-friendly while suppressing queer people at home, the statement said.
The statement called for an independent investigation into excessive and dehumanizing police enforcement, a public explanation, disciplinary action and an apology.
It called on police to disclose records of the operation, incorporate protections for marginalized groups into policing and accountability systems, and to stop stigmatizing LGBTQ venues and culture.
In response, the Wanhua Precinct said yesterday the operation was launched after it received a public complaint alleging the bar could be violating public decency laws.
The raid was conducted lawfully and did not discriminate toward LGBTQ people, it said, adding that the police obtained a court-approved search warrant after gathering evidence that the venue might have been contravening public decency laws.
There were 58 customers in the venue during the raid, and 51 were cited under the Social Order Maintenance Act (社會秩序維護法) for public nudity and indecent behavior, it said.
An officer did make an inappropriate remark to a person in a wheelchair and has been given a reprimand, the precinct said, adding it would continue to educate its officers to respect diversity while cracking down on illegal activity.
While critics have accused police of excessive use of force after officers entered the bar and ordered people inside to squat or kneel, sources said that given the large number of people at the scene, the orders were intended to secure the premises immediately, prevent anyone from assaulting officers, and ensure that evidence would not be concealed or destroyed.
As for allegations that police allowed a reporter into the bar to take sensational photographs, in violation of the principle of keeping investigations confidential, the source said the reporter was actually at the establishment as a customer at the time.
While some have accused police of conducting discriminatory inspections at two other gay bars later on Saturday night, the precinct said that the more than 20 locations inspected had been scheduled in advance. The inspections were unrelated to the afternoon raid and did not constitute discriminatory enforcement, it said.

Tuvalu dying ecosystem on front line of climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

When leaders visit the coral atolls that form the Pacific nation of Tuvalu on Tuesday, they will find a once-vibrant ecosystem wiped out due to climate change.
The pre-Conference of the Parties (COP) gathering, hosted by Fiji ahead of the annual UN climate conference in Turkey, has been billed as the Pacific’s chance to show the world first-hand the damage wrought by climate change in the vast ocean region.
Leaders are also set to spend a day on Tuvalu.
Photo:Reuters
There, scientists say, a marine heatwave in 2024 wiped out an estimated 99.9 percent of the coral that built the remote Tuvalu islands.
“You can swim for hours and hours along the reef in the lagoon, just skeleton after skeleton. It’s all dead,” said marine biologist Austin Bowden-Kerby, who visited last year and documented the devastation. “The very system that created the islands has died. It wasn’t pollution. It wasn’t overfishing. Just a direct result from climate change.”
Rising sea levels have largely swamped two of Tuvalu’s nine coral atolls — and scientists fear the entire archipelago could be unliveable by the end of the century.
Speaking at the UN last week, Tuvaluan Prime Minister Feleti Teo warned “sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality.”
Scientist Rajneel Singh said climate change was already impacting the waters that have long sustained Tuvalu’s population of 10,600.
“Elders used to fish for red snappers and other things,” he said. “It’s no longer frequent in the catch. And the sizes of the fish has been reduced as well.”
Bowden-Kerby said the lack of fish and the reduction in size is a serious concern for a country that lives off the sea.
“There are certain groups of fish that are dependent upon live corals,” he said. “Those fish are basically gone, and that’s the foundation of the food chain.”
A coral nursery is providing a faint glimmer of hope and has even seen the return of plankton-feeding fish.
They cannot replant all the lost reefs of Tuvalu, but they can protect some heat-resistant corals, Bowden-Kerby said.
That is if they have the money, which ran out at the end of last year.
“We need more funds just to sustain these things,” Singh said.
Bleaching events since 2018 have caused widespread coral mortality, with the UN World Ocean Assessment warning that 90 percent of reefs could disappear if global warming tops 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
What has happened to Tuvalu should serve as a lesson to others, scientists said.
Vanuatu and Samoa have moved to protect their corals from imminent bleaching.
Australia is being urged to take urgent action to protect its Great Barrier Reef.
Bowden-Kerby urged visiting Australians to see the dead reefs for themselves.
“You want to see what it looks like 10 years in the future? Tuvalu is a time machine for Australia.”
Only a handful of world leaders are expected to come to the pre-COP gathering in Fiji, let alone make the extra trip to Tuvalu.
“It does make you think nobody cares,” Singh said. “It’s very, very sad.”
And those that do come will likely stay for a quick photo-op before jumping back on their planes.
“No one is actually going out getting their feet wet and seeing what’s going on,” Singh said. “There’s a 10-minute flyover of the lagoon and that’s about it. There’s no awareness of what’s happening.”

The desktop survey, which began this month, will examine the number of facilities, the types of animals they house and the conditions they are held in, and how visitors interact with the animals. Exotic animal cafes, where visitors can interact with species ranging from otters to owls and marmots, have become popular attractions for Japanese and foreign tourists. However, researchers say some facilities keep threatened species, raising

The KMT’s referendum power grab is obvious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus’ proposed amendment to the Referendum Act (公民投票法), which it has made a legislative priority for this session, would not only bar the Central Election Commission (CEC) from refusing proposals submitted by the Legislative Yuan, but would also give national referendums the power to overturn Constitutional Court judgements. While proponents say the amendments would return power to the people, the proposals are actually a power grab to undermine the Executive Yuan and pave the way for a “supreme Legislative Yuan.” The KMT is also launching this calculated populist ploy to harvest political capital ahead of next month’s elections.
The amendment, proposed by KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) and others, would force the CEC to accept everything as submitted in a blatant assault on independent administrative review mechanisms. In practice, the core authority of any independent commission lies in its ability to operate free from political interference and conduct objective procedural and substantive reviews in strict accordance with the law.
The CEC is required to verify whether referendum proposals meet statutory requirements. If the law were amended to mandate that the CEC “may not refuse” any referendum proposal, it would effectively strip the commission of its statutory authority and allow the legislative majority to bypass legitimacy checks and force their proposals through.
Allowing a referendum to overturn a Constitutional Court judgement would effectively hollow out the constitutional review process and allow majority rule to override judicial independence.
The court safeguards democratic constitutionalism, shouldering the responsibility of revealing the blind spots of majority rule and protecting the rights of everyone. If an amendment to the Referendum Act could allow a majority vote to overturn a ruling of the highest constitutional authority, it would be a declaration that as long as legislators have the numbers, they do not need to abide by the Constitution. That would bring down Taiwan’s democratic safeguards, creating a breeding ground for populism.
Pushing ahead with the draft bill despite knowing it raises constitutional concerns is, in essence, generating conflict tailor-made for the Legislative Yuan. Should the legislative majority attempt to push through a controversial bill only to have it blocked or declared unconstitutional, it could immediately launch a referendum, endlessly prolonging the political battles with the judiciary and executive branch.
That strategy would inflame social divisions and incite hatred, while in the short term serving as a cheap mobilization tool to shore up a party’s base ahead of local elections.
The true value of a democratic system is that no institution possesses unchecked, absolute power. Faced with attempts by pan-blue and pan-white politicians to circumvent constitutional oversight through legislative amendments, voters must keep their eyes open and, when the elections arrive, use their ballots to remove these legislators who seek to undermine the constitution and disrupt political order, thereby protecting Taiwan’s democracy and freedom.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.

The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.
Indeed, the words “HELP” and “SOS” have been scratched out in the weeds now flourishing on the exposed lake bed.
The drought has ruined pleasure boat tourism, while some question whether the lake will ever return to enduring full health.
Photo: AFP
“It’s absolutely heartbreaking,” said historian David Favre, who lives in Les Brenets. “As children, we used to spend all our summers swimming at the beach, having fun by the water, diving, jumping in and sometimes even fishing.”
The Doubs river rises in the French Jura mountains and normally forms a lake at Les Brenets, where it begins to mark the border between France’s Franche-Comte region and Switzerland’s Neuchatel canton.
The lake ends at 27m-high waterfall, which has now stopped flowing.
The lake has dried up due to a combination of factors, including geological fissures that drain water underground, below-average rainfall and repeated heatwaves.
The months of June, July and August were each the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland since measurements began in 1864.
Every day Yvan Durig, owner and captain of the Lac des Brenets navigation company, measures the level of the remaining basin of water which is shrinking away at the very deepest bit of the lake.
“Normally, we have 25 or 30m of depth here,” but now there are only 9m of water left, and within it “the fish are really chock-a-block,” he said.
While locals are used to periods of low water, this spell is alarming, with the record low of 1906 set to be surpassed imminently.
A task force was set up by French and Swiss authorities in 2022, notably to explore ways of limiting the water draining into the fissures, but has not resulted in decisive action.
Pontoons and dozens of boats lie stranded on the dry lake bed.
The water level monitoring station for the lake is now so far out of the remaining basin that Durig does the measurements manually.
The water line is dropping about 20cm to 22cm a day.
On Thursday, it fell to an elevation of 735.34m above sea level — 14.66m below where it should be. Within days, it is expected to surpass the 1906 record drop of 15.35m.
A tiny stream now trickles through the weeds on the lake bed.
Maxime Fallet, who works at a Doubs riverboat excursion company, fears the lake is “destined to disappear.”
“The atmosphere in Les Brenets these days, when talk turns to the Doubs, is often tinged with a certain sadness, a melancholy at the thought that we could lose this lake — a lake that has been part of the soul of Les Brenets for generations,” he said.
Durig feels time is running out.
“We must take action... and seal the lakebed,” he said. “This can no longer take years.”

When Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) reported on the government’s six priority policy directions to the legislature during its opening session on Tuesday last week, he was not addressing a full house. All of the opposition lawmakers were absent during Cho’s 20-minute report, setting the tone for yet another executive-legislative standoff. The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) legislators only entered the chambers to vote down all 27 Control Yuan candidates nominated by President William Lai (賴清德).
The KMT caucus said its members’ absence was an act of “silent protest” against Cho, as he had refused to countersign several bills passed by the legislature. The TPP caucus said its members were elsewhere because Cho’s report was all fluff with no substance.
Meanwhile, the KMT caucus announced its priority legislation for the new session, including a bill to increase the government’s planned NT$10,000 per person cash handout to NT$20,000, amending the Criminal Code to allow caning as a punishment for certain crimes, and an amendment allowing national referendums to overturn Constitutional Court judgements and ban the Central Election Commission from reviewing or overruling referendum proposals initiated by the Legislative Yuan. They also include some bills that would significantly increase government spending, while benefiting only certain groups, such as making National Health Insurance free for elderly people.
In the four days since the new legislative session opened, the KMT caucus has made it clear that it would continue to be at odds with the Executive Yuan, pushing controversial bills and shelling out public funds to please voters.
While these standoffs give opposition lawmakers a sense of power and the impression that they can punish or retaliate against the Democratic Progressive Party, it is only short-lived, at the expense of national development and public welfare and interests, including those of the KMT’s and TPP’s supporters.
In the past two years, opposition lawmakers have been pushing to expand legislative power, but have failed as most of their bills were ruled unconstitutional. In an attempt to circumvent the judicial system, the opposition lawmakers crippled the Constitutional Court by raising the quorum for passing judgements and blocking nominees to fill court vacancies on the bench.
Allied KMT and TPP lawmakers also arbitrarily passed controversial bills that the Executive Yuan deemed unconstitutional and blamed Cho for not countersigning them, sometimes going as far as to threaten the Cabinet by stalling the review of the national budget.
The controversial bills sought to increase central government spending to benefit certain groups, which the Executive Yuan countered, citing Article 70 of the Constitution, which states that “the Legislative Yuan shall not make proposals for an increase in the expenditures in the budgetary bill presented by the Executive Yuan,” and with constitutional interpretations.
In 2024, the legislature forced the government to increase compensation to indigenous groups related to a logging ban. Last year, lawmakers stalled the review of the budget for a record-breaking 266 days, citing the government’s refusal to increase retirement income for police officers and firefighters. They also pushed the Executive Yuan to issue a nationwide NT$10,000 cash handout last year.
Bolstered by its previous success in pushing the central government to shell out public funding, the opposition-controlled legislature on Friday passed the first reading of the KMT caucus’ proposal of a NT$20,000 cash handout. It referred the bill to a committee for review, despite the Executive Yuan’s concern that it would raise national debt and crowd out funding for social welfare and major long-term policies.
However, the key point of contention between the ruling and opposition parties remains unaddressed. The KMT lawmakers are still eagerly trying to assert more power, encroaching upon executive authority by proposing bills to increase government spending and trampling on the Constitution with the amendment that would allow referendums to overturn Constitutional Court judgements. The opposition lawmakers’ rejection of all 27 Control Yuan candidates is also part of a greater plan to make legislative power overrule all other branches of government.
Disabling the Constitutional Court and the Control Yuan and hindering the Executive Yuan’s ability to execute its budget and policy might seem like victories to the opposition parties, so they are continuing this tactic in the new session. However, people are becoming tired of lawmakers habitually sabotaging the constitutional system. Opinion polls showed that trust in Lai has been growing, while trust levels for the KMT and TPP have been steadily dropping.

Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Share of drug offenders in prison dropping: agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

The percentage of inmates serving sentences for drug use has fallen over the past five years, largely due to community-based addiction treatment for people whose crimes were relatively minor, the Agency of Corrections said yesterday.
The government uses deferred prosecution with court-mandated addiction treatment and other community-based measures for people who use drugs without committing serious crimes, reducing unnecessary incarceration and limiting their contact with drug dealers in prison, the agency said.
Drug policies have drawn renewed debate after Democratic Progressive Party Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) proposed anti-drug measures for schools.
Photo: Chiang Chih-hsiung, Taipei Times
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) subsequently cited an article Shen wrote in 2014, asking whether he had advocated providing drugs and clean needles at community centers.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT, who is seeking re-election, said he supports methadone programs and the provision of clean needles, but opposes drug decriminalization and setting up community centers to provide drugs.
The two sides have over the past few days traded arguments over drug policy.
The third phase of the government’s New Generation Anti-Drug Strategy Action Plan, covering this year to 2028, draws on approaches adopted by other countries, and emphasizes differentiated referrals and a range of treatment options, Agency of Corrections data showed.
People whose cases primarily involve addiction and medical needs, and whose offenses are relatively minor, are given community-based treatment, while those who were involved in violence, serious crimes or other offenses are sent to correctional institutions, the agency said.
The approach allows people to receive the most appropriate treatment while reducing unnecessary incarceration and prison overcrowding, it said.
Agency data showed that 17,428 inmates were serving sentences for drug use in 2022, accounting for 35.1 percent of the total prison population of 49,720. That proportion fell to 33.2 percent in 2023, 31.7 percent in 2024 and 27.7 percent in last year.
As of June 30 this year, 14,521 inmates were serving sentences for drug use, accounting for 24.8 percent of the total 58,455 inmates, the data showed.
People who are sent to correctional institutions generally have more complex criminal circumstances, addiction problems and psychosocial needs, the agency said, adding that it is continuing its evidence-based drug offender treatment program and working with the Ministry of Health and Welfare on an integrated drug addiction treatment and quality improvement program in correctional institutions.
Since 2019, the agency has recruited psychologists and social workers, and formed interdisciplinary teams to expand services for inmates with high-risk needs, including addiction treatment.
Inmates in correctional institutions can also receive addiction treatment, the agency added.
People who complete deferred prosecution with mandated addiction treatment had a 66.3 percent lower risk of relapse compared with those who did not complete treatment, it said, citing research by the Crime Prevention Research Center at the Ministry of Justice’s Judicial Academy.
The agency said its overall policy emphasizes that targeted diversion and appropriate treatment are key to preventing recidivism.
Medical, psychological, social work and community resources should be coordinated in both settings to ensure that support continues after an inmate’s release, which would help reduce the risk of reoffense and help them reintegrate into society, it added.

The Taiwanese rivals later traded barbs on social media about the incident.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Caning as political theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

In 1904 the Japanese introduced caning to Taiwan. As a punishment, caning was applied by the Japanese to Taiwanese and Chinese subjects, never to the Japanese themselves (it had been outlawed in Japan in 1882). An imperial and colonial act, caning thus functioned to define and display social class boundaries.
So it is with the new legislation permitting caning proposed by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislators last week. According to the KMT proposal, individuals committing major fraud, aggravated sexual assault, driving under the influence of drugs and child abuse may be subject to caning. These are high-profile offenses that generate great public outrage.
The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) criticized the proposed legislation as populist. DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) put his finger on the social class element of the KMT’s bill, observing that caning would not be used for crimes committed by legislators, large-scale economic crimes and treason.
Photo: Lo Pei-te, Taipei Times
SINGAPORE AS MODEL
The KMT has long desired to turn Taiwan into Singapore, where caning is still practiced, an inheritance from British colonialism.
“Singapore is different from [Taiwan] as its emphasis is not on democratization. Nevertheless, it is professional, corruption-free and efficient, which is worth our learning,” said future president and KMT icon Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) in 2007 about his visit to Singapore.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Ma also mentioned, with a certain wistfulness, the much higher salaries of Singapore’s officials. Singapore was where Ma shook hands with PRC dictator Xi Jin-ping (習近平) in 2015. New Taipei City Mayor and failed KMT presidential candidate Hou You-yi (侯友宜) visited Singapore in 2023 on the eve of his presidential run.
Sure enough, the KMT legislator introducing this proposal not only pointed to Singapore as a model, but presented a Singapore citizen who had been caned twice as evidence that caning works. Track that: these KMT legislators thought a person whose first caning failed to change his ways was a model of how caning can work.
Note that other former colonies of the UK that practice caning, such as Malaysia and Brunei, are rarely exampled by caning advocates in Taiwan. Other former British colonies where caning was prominent deep into the 20th century, including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa, are also ignored for similar reasons. Singapore, on the other hand, is wealthy and run by Chinese, making it an acceptable ethnic and social class model for Taiwanese caning supporters.
Caning as criminal punishment retains a kind of enduring popularity. There is little evidence that it works to reduce crime, but it seems to make a certain kind of mind feel righteous and superior. When American teenager Michael Fay was caned in Singapore in 1994 (where people who overstay visas can be caned, a signal of how caning is used to enforce social class boundaries), the US government protested that it was a violation of international agreements on punishment and torture. Within the US, however, many state legislators called for its use.
SOCIAL CHAOS AND THE SCAPEGOAT
Proposals for caning long predate the current era. In 1997, at the height of the violent crime era, there were calls for flogging to be introduced as punishment. Singapore was identified as a model Taiwan should emulate. Then-minister of justice Liao Cheng-hao (廖正豪) said in July of that year that his ministry would consider flogging, if needed. To reassure the people that only criminals from the underclass would be flogged, Liao referenced the ongoing crackdown on gangsters.
DPP Legislator Hsueh Ling (薛凌), along with other DPP legislators, in 2007 proposed adding an amendment to the Sexual Assault Prevention Law (性侵害防治法) that contained language permitting caning for sexual offenders. The group was shot down by the Ministry of Justice, which said correctly that caning was a human rights violation that had no effect on recidivism.
Rene Girard, the insightful French thinker, argued in his book Violence and the Sacred that when social chaos threatens, societies attack the problem by arbitrarily selecting an individual for sacrifice. That person is then portrayed as both the cause of the problem, and the sacrifice through which it can be relieved: a scapegoat. That is how caning works: it turns criminals into human sacrifices whose suffering safely re-aligns the social disorder created by criminals, who represent the threat posed by the poor getting out of line.
That is why caning is invariably proposed in response to specific criminal actions that trigger public outrage, such as the heinous rape case used by DPP legislator Hsueh Ling (薛凌) to drive the 2007 proposal. It is never aimed at ubiquitous offenses such as criminal waste dumping, land theft, illegal factory construction, environmental pollution or embezzling money from one’s firm. Those are crimes committed by, or on behalf of, people with money.
Taiwan has outlawed corporal punishment in schools, because it has little positive effect, and as scholarship shows, simply makes children grow up to be more violent (see, for example, “Corporal punishment and violent behavior spectrum: A meta-analytic review” Frontiers in Psychology, Feb. 2024). The contrast between the calls for beating criminals with a bamboo stick and the treatment of children is striking, and shows how those proposals are simply calls for human sacrifice in an attempt to restore social boundaries.
WHY NOW?
Why is the KMT pushing a caning bill now? Taiwan is not in the midst of a violent crime wave — the vast majority of serious crime is white collar and kept beyond the public purview. The KMT has a huge problem: few of its policies have broad public appeal outside of its death penalty stand. The call for caning appears to exploit that public support for violent punishment of criminals at the bottom of the socio-economic hierarchy.
Like the death penalty, caning would have another effect. The EU, along with major international NGOs, protested the execution of Huang Lin-kai (黃麟凱) last year. Brutal punishments are out of step with global human rights standards. One KMT policy is using irritants that perturb Taiwan’s relations with other nations, like the way it uses the Senkaku Islands (also known as the Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台) claim to irritate Japan. Caning would likely be widely condemned as a regressive move, harming Taiwan’s relations with the advanced democracies.
It would also have other benefits. Once a caning law is in place, public pressure on the ruling DPP to use the law would grow, no doubt fanned by KMT attacks. The DPP will thus be placed in the awkward position of having to carry out inhumane punishments condemned by the international community, or fail to please local voters.
Of course, a media focusing on the absurd theatricality of caning legislation is a media that is not focused on the continued assault on governance by the KMT. Once this bill starts moving through the legislature, it will become a hot item in the media.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

Netanyahu, Miri Regev ‘celebrating failure’ after Flydubai hijacking attempt, Bennett says
Bennett and Eisenkot called for Transportation Minster Miri Regev to resign after the attempted hijacking
Opposition leaders have come out to condemn Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for celebrating the failure of the attempted hijacking of Flydubai Flight 1073, saying that any serious government would have fired the Transport Minister for allowing the attempt to happen at all on its watch.
Former Prime Minister and B'Yachad party chairman Naftali Bennett praised the heroes who stopped the hijacking, saying "We truly have a nation of lions." However, he quickly turned his eye to the government, saying that their "failure is terrible—shocking."
"Any reasonable government would have treated this incident as if a plane had crashed and 174 Israelis had been murdered," he continued. "Any prime minister who cares about Israel's security would have demanded answers from his Transportation Minister, Miri Regev, and fired her immediately."
"Instead of drawing lessons to prevent the next disaster, Netanyahu and Miri Regev are celebrating the failure that occurred on their watch," Bennett said.
Bennett further questioned Israelis’ safety, asking if any Iranian pilots had flown to Israel and drew a direct line from October 7 to this incident as another sign of the deteriorating security situation.
Former director general of the Ministry of Transportation and B'Yachad party candidate Keren Turner sharply criticised Regev, saying: "She is the one who chose to make a decision contrary to the position of the Shin Bet and the National Security Council that the Transportation Ministry’s security lacks the capacity to meet the required security standards. Yet, for the sake of a bit more authority and a few more political appointments, Miri Regev chose to endanger all our lives."
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot also came out to condemn the government and call for Miri Regev's resignation, saying, "In a proper, well-functioning government, the Minister of Transportation would have submitted her resignation yesterday evening. Since she failed to do so, the Prime Minister should have dismissed her immediately."
Eisenkot too, linked this failure to the government's failure to establish an independent inquiry into October 7, saying, "A clear line connects October 7th to the current failure: the culture of lies, cover-ups, and evasion of responsibility introduced by Benjamin Netanyahu and his ministers."

UK Green Party approves 'Zionism is racism' policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:37:02 UTC
01:37:02 KST

The UK's left-wing Green Party on Sunday voted to define Zionism as racism at its annual conference.
Members of the Green Party, which has five MPs in Britain's 650-seat parliament and has enjoyed gains in recent local elections and by-elections, backed the motion by 1,022 votes to 813.
Under the motion, Zionism would be "treated as any other form of racism", while the party supports the establishment of a "single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine".
"This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership," a Green Party spokesperson said.
The Greens have seen a surge in support under Zack Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government's stance on Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
The motion has also exposed divisions within the party. Polanski — who is currently running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer's London constituency — did not vote on the motion.
At least three of the party's five MPs opposed the motion, although Polanski said earlier this week that the "displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people" was "clearly racism".
Israel's Foreign Ministry condemned the decision, saying the policy went "far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate".
"Every political party in Britain, first and foremost the governing Labour Party, must unequivocally reject this twisted resolution," the ministry said.
UN investigators have concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, citing mass killings, serious bodily and mental harm, starvation and the systematic destruction of healthcare and education systems.
More than 73,500 Palestinians had been reported killed and over 174,000 injured since October 2023, while UN reporting has documented widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure across the besieged enclave.

Merz unveils fresh military aid in Kyiv, says Germany won’t be intimidated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:36:25 UTC
01:36:25 KST

Merz unveils fresh military aid in Kyiv, says Germany won’t be intimidated
KYIV - Germany will not be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Oct 4 as he announced a further €1 billion (S$1.4 billion) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv marked by Russian drone attacks.
Air-raid sirens and explosions rang out repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital as Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited a memorial to soldiers killed during the four-year-old war, as well as the Academy of Sciences where at least two people died in a drone strike last week.
Russia has escalated its drone attacks on Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks, targeting telecoms, electricity and transport infrastructure as well as military assets.
Speaking at a press conference alongside Zelensky, Merz said Moscow was trying to break the morale of the Ukrainian people, and announced €350 million for repairs in the energy sector. He said Germany remained Ukraine’s strongest backer.
Deals with German companies worth €6.5 billion
“We do this not only to protect Ukraine’s territorial integrity; we do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” Merz said, noting that Russia was carrying out cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns that struck at Europe’s democratic order.
“This demonstrates that we will not be intimidated,” he said.
Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
Officials said executives from German companies, who travelled with Merz, had signed 16 agreements with the Ukrainian government and businesses worth roughly €6.5 billion.
Among those deals, Ukraine inked an agreement with Germany’s Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems.
“What is important in this visit is that not only Germany is helping Ukraine, but Ukraine is sharing its knowledge, experience, as well as orders,” Zelensky said. “These are jobs for Germany.”
Zelensky praised a new jet drone interceptor, dubbed SPYS and developed by Quantum, for showing promising results. He said Ukraine and Germany were close to finalising a broad defence deal, which he has previously said would include the production of drones, missiles and related software.
Zelensky vows to respond
Since the summer, Russia has targeted civilian and military infrastructure daily with dozens of high-speed jet-powered attack drones – which Ukraine has struggled to down because they are much faster than previous propeller versions.
One of the Russian strikes on Oct 4 hit the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, damaging its roadway, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. The explosion injured two people and damaged a hot water supply system in the area, he said.
Zelensky said Russia’s decision to escalate air strikes against infrastructure targets was due to setbacks it had suffered on the battlefield, and he vowed that Ukraine would retaliate. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin wanted to force residents to flee Ukraine’s major cities.
“If our bridges collapse, we will manage to get out of this situation, but his people will feel it too ... This is maximum escalation of this war,” Zelensky told reporters.
Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since last week in an effort to disrupt links between the capital’s two sides and logistics routes between central and eastern Ukraine.
Merz appeals for end to ‘senseless war’
Zelensky said US peace envoy Steve Witkoff has messaged him to urge a return to trilateral talks as soon as possible. He said Ukraine was willing to meet this month and hoped Russia would join, but he said Western allies need to apply more pressure to Moscow to bring the war to an end.
Earlier in the day, during the visit to the badly damaged Academy of Sciences, Merz appealed to Putin to “put an end to this senseless war”.
“We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop,” the German leader said.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said on Oct 3 that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against travelling to Ukraine. REUTERS

Le calendrier chargé d’Emmanuel Macron complique sa venue à la COP31
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:35:13 UTC
01:35:13 KST

Le calendrier chargé d’Emmanuel Macron complique sa venue à la COP31
Bien qu’il aime se poser en défenseur de l’Accord de Paris sur le climat, le chef de l’Etat ne semble plus placer les négociations climatiques en haut de ses priorités calendaires.
Pour le moment, l’intérêt d’Emmanuel Macron pour le grand raout des discussions climatiques demeure timide. | Pool photo par Ludovic Marin via AFP/Getty Images
PARIS — Ira ou n’ira pas ? Emmanuel Macron laisse planer le doute sur sa participation à la COP31 — la dernière de son double mandat —, qui aura lieu à Antalya, en Turquie.
Ce pourrait être mal engagé : prévu les 11 et 12 novembre, le sommet des dirigeants de la COP31, qui rassemble traditionnellement les chefs d’Etat et de gouvernement, se chevauche avec les commémorations de la fin de la Première Guerre mondiale et le Forum de Paris sur la paix. Ce conflit d’agenda complique la venue du président français, indiquent à POLITICO deux conseillers de l’exécutif.
La possibilité d’un déplacement en Turquie, pays hôte, le 12 novembre — et donc d’un passage express à la COP — n’est toutefois pas complètement exclue à ce stade. “Si ça se trouve, il a déjà décidé qu’il y allait”, tempère ainsi l’un des conseillers mentionnés plus haut.
Advertisement
Reste que pour le moment, l’intérêt d’Emmanuel Macron pour le grand raout des discussions climatiques demeure timide : invité à prendre part à la pré-COP, qui se tiendra du lundi 3 au jeudi 8 octobre aux Fidji, il a laissé la priorité à sa ministre de la Transition écologique, Monique Barbut.
De “Make our planet great again” au détricotage
Cette attitude tranche avec les débuts au pouvoir de celui qui se plaçait alors en héritier de l’Accord de Paris, dont l’objectif est de contenir le réchauffement climatique “bien en dessous” de 2 °C. A peine un mois après son élection, en juin 2017, le président de la République avait ainsi trouvé un écho international en prononçant le discours “Make our planet great again”, en réponse à Donald Trump qui venait d’annoncer le (premier) retrait des Etats-Unis du traité.
Dix ans plus tard, les avancées écologiques du premier quinquennat ont pour partie été détricotées lors du second, sur la rénovation thermique des bâtiments ou la lutte contre l’artificialisation des sols, entre autres. Ces reculs ont eu des conséquences sur l’influence de la France sur la scène internationale, analysait auprès de POLITICO, en juin 2025, Arnaud Gilles, ancien porte-parole du WWF et spécialiste des questions environnementales.
Le risque d’une image ternie à l’international
Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’Emmanuel Macron laisse planer le doute sur sa venue au sommet mondial sur le climat. L’an dernier, il avait officialisé son intention de s’y rendre un peu plus d’une semaine avant l’événement. Il n’était finalement resté que quelques heures sur place, à Belém, le temps d’une escale entre deux visites d’Etat au Brésil et au Mexique. Il s’était également montré discret lors des célébrations du 10e anniversaire des Accords de Paris.
Une impasse sur le dernier sommet mondial sur le climat de son mandat viendrait écorner un peu plus l’image de champion de l’écologie qu’Emmanuel Macron cherche à renvoyer à l’international. D’autres n’ont pas traîné pour officialiser leur participation. Le Premier ministre britannique, le travailliste Andy Burnham, l’a annoncée dès sa première allocution parlementaire, début septembre, après son accession au pouvoir.

Ukrainian drones deliver new batch of food to Russian-occupied Oleshky
KYIV, Oct 4 - Ukraine's military has again used drones to deliver food and medicines to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday.
Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.

Saddam Haftar drone claims threaten US Libya unity push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:32:16 UTC
01:32:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Saddam Haftar drone claims threaten Washington's Libya unity push
A US-backed effort to reunify Libya is facing a major setback after figures linked to the Tripoli government accused Saddam Haftar of overseeing a cell responsible for drone attacks on vital energy infrastructure in western Libya.
Sources in Libya's Government of National Unity (GNU) said suspects arrested over a series of attacks on oil and electricity facilities in August had been working for Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based Libyan National Army (LNA) and son of its commander Khalifa Haftar.
"No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam," GNU sources told The Guardian.
The allegations, which have not been independently verified, could undermine a US-led initiative that has placed Saddam Haftar at the centre of efforts to bridge Libya's longstanding east-west divide.
US President Donald Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, has been leading the initiative, which seeks to unify Libya's rival political, economic and security institutions.
Haftar travelled to Washington in June, where he met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to discuss unifying Libya's military.
"The US will continue working with Libyan leaders and international partners to support a more peaceful, unified and prosperous Libya," Rubio said following the meeting.
Media reports have suggested Washington has explored a power-sharing arrangement involving Haftar and Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, whose GNU controls much of western Libya.
No agreement has been formally announced, and Boulos has denied that his initiative is designed to entrench Libya's dominant political families.
"It's not about families or names," Boulos previously said of reports surrounding the proposal.
The new allegations centre on a string of unprecedented drone attacks in August against infrastructure in and around Zawiya, around 45 kilometres west of Tripoli.
Explosive-laden drones repeatedly targeted the city's strategically important oil complex, including a petrol storage tank containing approximately 4.5 million litres of fuel.
Other strikes hit electricity infrastructure, contributing to blackouts in western Libya and adding to public anger over already unreliable power supplies.
No group claimed responsibility for the attacks at the time.
Libyan authorities announced in September that they had dismantled what they described as an organised "sabotage cell" accused of using suicide drones to attack oil tanks in Tripoli and Zawiya as well as Zawiya's power station.
The GNU initially said five Libyan and foreign suspects had been arrested.
The Guardian reported that three detained Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the LNA's Tariq bin Ziyad Brigade and that GNU sources now believe the group was operating on Saddam Haftar's behalf.
The newspaper also reported claims that the alleged plot extended to a planned attack on Tripoli airport.
The allegations have not been publicly substantiated, while earlier analysis of the Zawiya attacks pointed to the city's complex web of rival armed groups as another possible context.
Zawiya has witnessed repeated fighting between local militias competing for territorial control and influence over the illicit economy, including lucrative fuel-smuggling networks.
The claims nevertheless threaten to complicate Washington's attempt to bridge a political division that has endured for more than a decade.
Libya has effectively been divided between rival eastern and western authorities since renewed civil war erupted in 2014, three years after the overthrow of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Khalifa Haftar controls much of eastern and southern Libya through the LNA, while Dbeibah's internationally recognised government is based in Tripoli.
Washington's initiative is running alongside a separate UN-backed political process aimed at overcoming the institutional split and ultimately holding national elections.
The allegations against Saddam Haftar could also affect that process and intensify competition within the Haftar family over who will eventually succeed the 82-year-old eastern commander.
Saddam is widely regarded as a leading potential successor to his father and has assumed an increasingly prominent military and diplomatic role.
But his brothers Khaled and Belqasim have also emerged as influential figures within eastern Libya's political and military establishment, amid growing competition over the future leadership of the Haftar camp.

The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:30:32 UTC
01:30:32 KST

“To the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference. Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’s manifesto promise to “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”.
In its modern form, leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests – billionaires, aristocrats and big businesses – that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now £2,405, up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than £7,000 a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers are increasingly bypassing flats.
The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a £250 annual cap on ground rents for existing residential leases and limits on fees for requests such as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less to buy out freeholds. But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change?
The issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Six out of seven homes sold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue a concrete test of Labour’s credibility. The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded in Berlin and across Spain.
It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has already won against them in the courts when defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of the existing 5m leasehold homes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.

Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP

Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP
WFP food aid truck attacked in Sudan’s South Kordofan, killing one driver as violence escalates in the region.
An air strike on United Nations trucks has killed a driver in Sudan’s South Kordofan, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).
The WFP said in a statement released on Sunday that the trucks, carrying food aid, were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles” as they came under attack. The agency did not identify those responsible.
The strike hit the convoy on Saturday as it was travelling between two cities controlled by the government’s Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in South Kordofan state.
Fighting in the Kordofan region intensified in late 2025, turning the territory into a strategic battleground between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The two have been fighting for control of Sudan in a civil war that has now lasted more than three years.
The extent of the damage and additional details regarding the attack on WFP aid trucks are still being assessed. The UN agency said that it has called for an investigation.
“These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need,” the statement reads.
Since the war began in April 2023, one in five attacks in Sudan has occurred in the Kordofan region. The army has the upper hand in the north, having made a series of recent gains, while the RSF maintains control over much of the west. South Kordofan remains contested.
Both the SAF and RSF have increasingly deployed drones in their war, with attacks on towns in North Kordofan growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian infrastructure coming under attack across the region.
The civil war has forcibly displaced 14 million people, plunging the country into one of the worst modern food crises and killing tens of thousands of people.
Nearly 19.5 million people – about 41 percent of Sudan’s population – were struggling with acute food crises between February and May, according to an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification assessment, a leading authority on global hunger. More than five million faced extreme, life-threatening food shortages, and 135,000 were at risk of famine.

Saeidi Brothers release reimagined folk single “Sar-e Dast-e Yarom”
TEHRAN- Iranian traditional vocalist brothers Ali and Mohammad Saeidi have released their latest single, “Sar-e Dast-e Yarom” (“My Beloved’s Cuff”), a reimagined version of an old Iranian folk song.
The piece, performed by the Saeidi brothers, draws on a traditional folk composition attributed to Hossein Kouhi Kermani, and is based on the rendition of maestro Mohammad-Taghi Saeidi.
According to the artists, the song is rooted in a folk narrative associated with fashion and the period when modern fashion began making its way into Iranian society. The brothers have sought to preserve the character of the old folk material while developing it through a contemporary musical arrangement, and the track is presented as an expanded reinterpretation rather than a straightforward revival of the original.
In the new release, Mojtaba Mojtaba Abolqasempour is credited with playing santur and electronic instruments, as well as arranging, mixing and mastering the piece, while Majid Mazaheri plays the kamancheh.
Ali and Mohammad Saeidi, born in Isfahan in 1981, are twin traditional Iranian singers who studied Persian vocal techniques and the radif repertoire with masters including Mohammad-Taghi Saeidi, Mohammad Ali Kianinejad and Fazlollah Shahzamani. Their work has included concerts in Iran and abroad as well as recordings drawing on traditional Iranian music.
The brothers previously launched a short-song project aimed at introducing Iranian traditional music and art to audiences with limited time, producing brief musical videos based on selections from the Persian traditional repertoire.
Their collaboration with internationally known Iranian composer and conductor Ali Rahbari has also included the orchestral project “Persian Nightingales.”

“The Long Winter”, a 44-minute documentary, tells the story of an elderly couple living in a village in northern Iran. The 10th edition of Eurasia.Doc was held from September 28 to October 2 in Smolensk, Russia, and Minsk, Belarus. According to the festival’s official website, 361 films from 14 countries were submitted to the main competition, with 34 works eventually selected for the final competition.
The festival brought together documentary filmmakers, journalists, experts and audiences from several countries, with films addressing historical events, contemporary social issues, human experiences and developments in different societies.
